- **Approve all and start calling** is the approval for every call on the list, so the calls don't wait for a person again, even while the teammate is training.
- The same pace (calls an hour), open hours, quiet hours, **Pause**, **Resume** and **Stop** as texts. Each call is an AI call like the others (see "AI calls" below): recorded, the business's voicemail choice, "don't call me again" respected. Each person's row shows how their call went: **Calling soon**, **Talked** (with the summary), **Voicemail**, **No answer**, **Busy**, **Not called**.
- It pauses itself, saying why, when the AI teammate isn't taking calls (off, or its phone off).

Needs `20261008000200_quote_and_campaign_calls.sql` (`campaigns.channel` `call`, `campaigns.call_opening`). See "Apply new migrations".

**About an offer**: a campaign can be about one of the business's offers (Knowledge → Offers, live or upcoming). Picking one fills in the goal if it's empty, and the AI writes each text from the offer's own words and says when it ends. An archived offer can't be picked.

### Offer ending

| Row              | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | On to begin with |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| **Offer ending** | A card on Home from the start of the day three days before an offer's last day, urgent on the last day. **Open the offers** goes to Knowledge → Offers to extend it; it closes when the offer is extended past that window, archived or over | Yes              |

Needs `20261006000200_offers_in_campaigns.sql` (the `offer_lapsing` card kind and `campaigns.offer_id`). See "Apply new migrations".

### AI calls

The AI teammate can ring a customer itself. Three reasons, each a row on **Settings → Automations**, off to begin
with, and call campaigns (see "Outreach campaigns" above):

| Row                                   | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | On to begin with |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| **Call to confirm tomorrow’s visit**  | Three hours after the day-before reminder asked them to confirm, if they still haven't, it calls. A "yes" on the call confirms the visit. Never within two hours of the start                                                       | No               |
| **Call back a missed call**           | Five minutes after a customer's call nobody (and no AI) answered, it calls back, unless anyone has been in touch with them since. Not for a call more than a day old                                                                | No               |
| **Call about a quote with no answer** | Two days after a quote's reminder text, if it's still open (no yes or no, not expired) and they haven't texted, emailed or called since, it asks to call. **Always waits for a person to approve it**, whatever the teammate's mode | No               |

All three need the AI teammate on, with its phone turned on (**AI team → Phone**); the row says so until then.
The quote call comes after the quote's reminder text (Settings → Payments, "Nudge an estimate nobody answered"); with no
reminder set, there's no call either.

- **Every call** comes from the business number, in open hours only and never in quiet hours (it waits for the next
  good moment). It starts: "Hi Ann, this is Ava, an AI assistant for Lone Star HVAC. This call is recorded. I'm
  calling about …". The call is recorded (both sides), and its words are on the customer's timeline like any call.
- **While the teammate is training,** each call waits for a person: a card on **Workflows → Approvals** ("Ava asks
  to call Ann") and Home's "Drafts awaiting review". **Approve the call** places it at the next good moment; **Reject**
  means no call. One nobody decides before it expires isn't made.
- **When a voicemail box answers** (the carrier can tell): what the business chose in the row's **Adjust** — hang
  up and send a text instead (the default), leave a short message, or just hang up.
- **"Don't call me again"** on a call: the AI records it, and no AI call goes to them after that. The customer page's
  Details has **Calls from us** ("Agreed in writing (Signed service agreement)", "Doesn't want calls", "Not asked"),
  where a person can change it. A yes needs where it's written; campaign calls only go to a yes.
- **On a quote call** the AI knows the quote's name, total and last day. It answers questions from those and what
  the business knows, never changes a price or the terms, and for going ahead points to the link in the text they
  got (the team can text it again).

Kept in `app.ai_calls` (one row per call: why, status, how it went, the summary) and `people.call_consent`; a call
waiting for approval is an AI teammate draft of kind `call`. The worker's jobs are `ai_calls.consider`,
`ai_calls.place` and `ai_calls.voicemail_text`; the carrier asks `/webhooks/twilio/voice/ai-call` what to do when
it's answered. Needs `20261008000100_ai_calls.sql` and, for quote and campaign calls,
`20261008000200_quote_and_campaign_calls.sql`. See "Apply new migrations".

**When something goes wrong**

- **No calls go out:** check the row is on, the teammate is on with its phone on, the business has a live number,
  and the balance has room. An `ai_calls` row says why a call was left alone (`reason`: `already_confirmed`,
  `in_touch_since`, `no_calls`, `switched_off`, `no_voice`, `balance`, `no_number`, `too_late`, and for campaign
  calls `no_call_consent` and `campaign_stopped`).
- **A call rings but the AI says nothing:** the voice agent isn't set up (`VOICE_AGENT` on the worker); the call
  hangs up by itself.

### Tags and contact details, kept up to date by the AI

Two rows under **Pipeline and records**, and **Settings** → **Tags** for the whole list:

| Row                                 | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | On to begin with |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| **Tag customers for you**           | Three minutes after a customer's message (either way), call transcript, visit booked, done or cancelled, deal opened, won or lost, quote answered, bill paid, plan started or form filled in, the AI reads everything the business knows about them and puts on the business's tags that fit, or takes off ones HandsFreeOS put on that no longer do. At most one look per customer every 30 minutes | Yes              |
| **Keep contact details up to date** | In the same look, fills in or fixes their name, email, number and address when they said so ("my new email is…", "we moved to…")                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Yes              |

What it will never do, whatever the AI answers (the rules are in code, `packages/core/src/contact-ai/rules.ts`, not only in the prompt):

- **Make up a tag.** Only the business's own tags, matched by name, and on a pass only the ones it was given.
- **Take off a tag a person put on.** It takes off only tags HandsFreeOS put on (itself, a workflow, the AI teammate).
- **Write a detail nobody gave.** A new email, number, name or address must appear in what the customer or the team actually wrote or said: texts, emails, call transcripts, form answers, notes. Never a website chat whose visitor didn't prove who they are (a code, M18), never the AI teammate's own words.
- **Lose what was on file.** A main email or number it replaces moves to the other emails or numbers, labelled **Previous**.

**Adjust** holds **How you tag customers**: a few lines in the business's words ("VIP: has spent over $2,000 with us") the AI reads every time (`workspaces.settings.automations.contactAi.guide`).

**Going through everyone you already have.** **Settings** → **Tags** → **Let the AI tag your customers** (owners and admins: `tags.manage`), or ask the Assistant ("tag everyone who asked about solar as Solar interest"). Say what to look for, which tags it may use (all of them by default), only the customers with one tag if you like, and whether it also fixes contact details. It goes through them in the background, 10 at a time, with its progress on the page and a **Stop**. When today's AI limit or the balance runs out it waits and carries on by itself an hour later. One pass runs at a time. A big list uses the AI for every customer, so it can take more than a day's allowance.

**Workflows that start on tag changes** (**Tags change on a customer or lead**) start for every customer the AI tags. The Assistant's card says which ones before anyone agrees; check with the client before a pass over a big list.

**Everything is written down twice.** Each change is a command like a person's (`record.set_tags` for each tag, `person.update` for details) with its event and audit row: the audit log shows **HandsFreeOS AI** (actor `system`, channel `contact_ai`, `_contactAi` on the event) with the AI's reason under **Reason**. And every look it takes, changed or not, is a row of `app.contact_ai_reviews`: what the AI said, what was done, and what was left alone and why. **Settings** → **Tags** shows the latest changes with their reasons; the Assistant's `ai_tagging_status` reads the same log. Passes are rows of `app.contact_ai_sweeps`; the worker's jobs are `contact_ai.review` and `contact_ai.sweep`. The AI's tokens count as `automations` in `app.ai_usage`, inside the daily limit.

**The Assistant, when asked.** Beside the pass, the Assistant can list many customers at once with their tags (`list_customers`, also "without this tag"), put tags on or take them off up to 200 customers in one card (`tag_customers`, making a new tag on the way), and change, add or take off any detail of one customer, the business's own fields included (`update_customer`). Each waits for Confirm, runs as the person ("via Assistant"), and keeps the reason they gave on every audit row.

Needs `20261007000600_the_ai_keeps_customers_tidy.sql`. See "Apply new migrations". Locally, `ASSISTANT_PROVIDER=scripted` makes the stand-in put on any listed tag a customer's history names, take off one they say they're "no longer" into, and take "my new email is …", "my new number is …" and "we moved to …" as details.

## Who can do what: roles and permissions

Everyone in a business has a role: **Owner**, **Admin** or **Member**. Each role comes with a set of things it can
do, and an owner can change that set for their business (migration 0106). Nothing here needs setting up: the
defaults are what the roles always did.

- **For a role:** **Settings** → **Permissions** lists every permission in six groups (Customers, Inbox and calls,
  Calendar, Money, Automations and AI, Business and team), with a column for **Admins** and one for **Members**.
  Each is left at **Default**, or turned **On** or **Off**. A choice saves as soon as it is picked, and **Reset
  admins** or **Reset members** puts a whole column back.
- **For one person:** **Members** → the three dots next to them → **Permissions**. The same list, where each is left
  as **Same as their role**, or turned **On** or **Off** just for them. What is set for a person wins over what is
  set for their role. They get an **Own permissions** badge, and the Permissions page lists them at the bottom.
- **Owners always do everything,** and only owners see the Permissions page. There is nothing to set for an owner:
  to limit someone, make them an admin or a member first.
- **Some permissions need others.** Sending invoices needs seeing bills; managing all money needs both. Turning one
  on while what it needs is off does nothing, and the page says so under the picker ("Off until “See bills for
  their work” is on").
- **What never changes:** opening the business and seeing its customers and team are part of every role; deleting
  the business and setting permissions stay with owners.

**Letting members bill.** Turn **Send estimates and invoices, start plans** on for Members, or for one person. They
can then write, send and void estimates and invoices, take a cash or check payment, and start and run plans — for
the customers they're on (as the main person or on the team), the leads assigned to them and the visits they work,
and only into the payment accounts they may use. Refunds, products, money settings, payment accounts and the whole
business's totals stay with **Manage all money**. On the phone they send and take payments for their own jobs; plans
are on the web.

**How it holds.** The database works out what each person may do from their role, the business's settings and
their own, and keeps the answer in one place (`app.workspace_access.permissions`). Every check reads it: the API,
the row security on every table, the worker, and what the phone app syncs — money reaches a phone's whole-business
copy only for someone who manages it (`manages_money`). A change takes effect at once, for everyone it touches.

**When something goes wrong**

- **Someone says a button disappeared:** look for an **Own permissions** badge next to them in **Members**, and at
  their role's column in **Settings** → **Permissions**. Every change is in the audit log ("turned “Send estimates
  and invoices, start plans” off for Marco").
- **"You can bill the customers you’re on"**: see **When something goes wrong** under Money, next.

## Money: Stripe and Square

HandsFreeOS takes money for a business, not from it. **Each business signs into its own Stripe or Square account** in **Settings** → **Payments**. Their customers' payments land in that business's own balance. They are the merchant of record: the payouts are theirs, the fees are theirs, the chargebacks and the refunds are theirs, and they can revoke our access from their own dashboard at any time without asking us. HandsFreeOS never holds their money and never sees a card number — the customer's card details go from the customer's own browser straight to the provider, and only a token comes back.

What you set up here is the **platform**: one Stripe Connect platform and one Square developer application, both owned by HandsFreeOS, which is what lets a business click Connect and sign in. Every value goes on `handsfreeos-worker`. The API refuses to start if it holds any variable starting with `STRIPE_`, `SQUARE_`, `PAYMENTS_`, `PAYPAL_`, `NMI_` or `AUTHORIZE_NET_`, and none of them ever goes in Vercel or GitHub.

The same Stripe account is used a second way, in the other direction: it is what a business's **usage
top-up** is charged to, which is how HandsFreeOS gets paid. That needs no extra account, key or webhook —
see "Usage balances: what businesses pay us", Part 0.

Money needs the migrations `20260920000100_money_catalog.sql` to `20260920001000_refunds_close.sql`. See "Apply new migrations".

Without any of this, everything else in HandsFreeOS works. **Settings** → **Payments** simply says the provider isn't set up, and a business can still write estimates and invoices and record cash, cheques and card payments they took themselves.

### Before you start

- A Stripe account for HandsFreeOS itself, with you as an administrator. Stripe Connect has to be enabled on it (Stripe asks a few questions about what your platform does).
- A Square account for HandsFreeOS itself, and access to the Square Developer dashboard with it.
- The business details Stripe and Square ask a platform for: legal company name, address, website and what the software does.
- The worker already running at `https://hooks.handsfreeos.com` (Fly Part 8). **Both providers check a webhook address before they save it**, so the webhooks come after the worker is live.
- Your password manager, open, so every value goes straight into it.

#### Order of work

Do Stripe Parts 1 to 5, then Square Parts 1 to 5, then the checks. Stripe's Connect application review can take a few days, so **start it first** and do everything else while you wait. Square's sandbox works immediately; its production application also needs Square to look at it before other people's accounts may connect.

Nothing here is per-client. A business connects its own account from inside the app, and that takes a minute.

### Stripe Part 1: Turn Connect on

1. Sign in to the Stripe dashboard as HandsFreeOS.
2. Go to **Connect** in the left menu and press **Get started**.
3. Choose the **standard** account type when asked how your platform works: each business keeps its own full Stripe account and its own dashboard, which is the point.
4. Fill in the platform profile Stripe asks for: what HandsFreeOS does, the kinds of business that use it, and your website.

You should see Connect appear in the dashboard's left menu with a **Platform settings** page under it. Stripe may take a few days to approve the profile. You can finish the rest and test in test mode meanwhile.

### Stripe Part 2: The platform's client id and its branding

1. Go to **Settings** → **Connect** → **Platform settings** (search the dashboard for "Platform settings" if it has moved).
2. Under **OAuth settings**, copy the **Client ID**. It starts with `ca_`.
3. Save it in your password manager as "Stripe Connect platform", under Client ID.
4. On the same page, add the **redirect URI**:

   ```text
   https://hooks.handsfreeos.com/oauth/stripe/callback
   ```

5. Set the platform name, icon and brand colour under **Branding**. This is what a business sees on Stripe's own sign-in screen, so it should say HandsFreeOS.

You should see the redirect URI listed and saved. Stripe refuses the sign-in outright if the address the worker sends does not match this one exactly, including `https` and the trailing path.

### Stripe Part 3: The API keys

1. Go to **Developers** → **API keys**.
2. Copy the **live secret key**. It starts with `sk_live_`.
3. Save it in your password manager as "Stripe Connect platform", under secret key. **This key can move money in every connected account.** It goes on the worker and nowhere else.
4. Copy the **live publishable key**. It starts with `pk_live_`. It is not a secret — it is sent to customers' browsers on purpose — but keep it with the rest.
5. Save it under publishable key.
6. Switch the dashboard to **test mode** (the toggle at the top) and copy the test versions of both keys.
7. Save those as a separate entry, "Stripe test keys". They are for your laptop only.

### Stripe Part 4: The Connect webhook

Do this after the worker is live at `https://hooks.handsfreeos.com` (Fly Part 8). Stripe calls the address before it saves it.

**Check which environment you are in first.** Stripe gives you three, not two: live, the account's own test mode, and any **sandbox**, which is a separate account with its own id and its own webhooks. An endpoint built in a sandbox is invisible to live and to test mode, and its signing secret verifies nothing outside it. The endpoint list on each is the only way to be sure — a sandbox looks exactly like test mode while you are in it. You need one on live before a real business can be paid.

1. Go to **Developers** → **Webhooks**.
2. Press **Add endpoint**, and choose **Connect** (events from connected accounts), not **Account**.
3. Endpoint URL:

   ```text
   https://hooks.handsfreeos.com/webhooks/stripe
   ```

4. Select these events, and no others. They are exactly the ones the worker acts on; anything else is answered with a 200 and dropped.
   - `payment_intent.succeeded`, `payment_intent.processing`, `payment_intent.amount_capturable_updated`, `payment_intent.payment_failed`, `payment_intent.canceled`
   - `charge.refunded`, `refund.updated`, `charge.refund.updated`, `charge.dispute.created`, `charge.dispute.updated`, `charge.dispute.closed`
   - `invoice.paid`, `invoice.payment_succeeded`, `invoice.payment_failed`
   - `customer.subscription.created`, `customer.subscription.updated`, `customer.subscription.paused`, `customer.subscription.resumed`, `customer.subscription.deleted`
   - `account.updated`, `capability.updated`, `account.application.deauthorized`
5. Set the endpoint's **API version** to the one the worker pins (`API_VERSION` in `apps/worker/src/payments/stripe.ts`, today `2026-08-26.dahlia`). Stripe otherwise sends events shaped by the account's default version, which would drift away from the version the code reads them with.
6. Press **Add endpoint**.
7. On the endpoint's page, press **Reveal** under **Signing secret** and copy it. It starts with `whsec_`.
8. Save it in your password manager as "Stripe Connect platform", under webhook signing secret. **Each environment has its own**: a sandbox secret refuses every live event with a 403, and the log says `rejected an unsigned or mis-signed payment webhook`.

You should see the endpoint listed as enabled. `account.application.deauthorized` is the one that matters most for trust: it is how a business revoking us in their own Stripe dashboard is noticed here, and the connection is marked disconnected without anybody having to tell us.

### Stripe Part 5: A test account to connect

You need a connected account of your own to try a real round trip with.

1. Switch the dashboard to **test mode**.
2. Go to **Connect** → **Accounts** → **Create**, or simply run the connect flow from a HandsFreeOS workspace and sign in with a new test account when Stripe offers it.
3. Use Stripe's test card `4242 4242 4242 4242` with any future expiry and any CVC when you pay.

Stripe's own test cards are listed under **Developers** → **Test data**.

### Square Part 1: The developer application

1. Sign in at the Square Developer dashboard with HandsFreeOS's Square account.
2. Press **+** to make an application. Name it `HandsFreeOS`.
3. Open the application, and note the environment switch at the top: **Sandbox** and **Production** have **different** credentials, and you will need both.

### Square Part 2: The credentials

1. With the switch on **Production**, open **Credentials**.
2. Copy the **Application ID** and the **Application Secret**.
3. Save both in your password manager as "Square developer application".
4. Switch to **Sandbox** and copy the sandbox Application ID and secret.
5. Save those as a separate entry, "Square sandbox". They are for your laptop only.

### Square Part 3: The redirect

1. Open **OAuth** in the application's left menu, with the switch on **Production**.
2. Set the **Redirect URL**:

   ```text
   https://hooks.handsfreeos.com/oauth/square/callback
   ```

3. Save.
4. Switch to **Sandbox** and set the same field to your laptop's address (see "Trying a real provider from your laptop"), or leave it until you need it.

HandsFreeOS asks a seller for these permissions, and Square refuses the whole sign-in if one is left unticked: `MERCHANT_PROFILE_READ`, `PAYMENTS_READ`, `PAYMENTS_WRITE`, `CUSTOMERS_READ`, `CUSTOMERS_WRITE`, `SUBSCRIPTIONS_READ`, `SUBSCRIPTIONS_WRITE`, `ITEMS_READ`, `ITEMS_WRITE`. The seller sees them listed on Square's own screen.

### Square Part 4: The webhook

Do this after the worker is live at `https://hooks.handsfreeos.com` (Fly Part 8).

1. Open **Webhooks** → **Subscriptions**, with the switch on **Production**.
2. Press **Add subscription**. Name it `HandsFreeOS`.
3. URL:

   ```text
   https://hooks.handsfreeos.com/webhooks/square
   ```

4. Choose the API version Square offers as current, and select these events, which are the ones the worker acts on:
   - `payment.created`, `payment.updated` — Square has no "payment failed" event and no separate "succeeded" one, so where the money is has to be read off the payment itself
   - `refund.created`, `refund.updated`
   - `dispute.created`, `dispute.state.updated`, `dispute.evidence.created`
   - `invoice.payment_made`
   - `subscription.created`, `subscription.updated`
   - `location.updated`
   - `oauth.authorization.revoked`

   Older guides name `dispute.state.changed`, `dispute.evidence.added` and `merchant.updated`. Square no longer offers them: the first two are the old names of the dispute events above, and the Merchants API has no webhooks. The worker still reads the two old dispute names if they ever arrive.

5. Save, then copy the **Signature Key** from the subscription's page.
6. Save it in your password manager as "Square developer application", under webhook signature key.
7. Do the same in **Sandbox** if you will test from your laptop, and keep that signature key separate.

`oauth.authorization.revoked` is Square's equivalent of Stripe's deauthorized event: it is how a seller revoking us in their own Square dashboard is noticed here.

### Square Part 5: A sandbox seller to connect

1. In the developer dashboard, open **Sandbox** → **Test accounts**.
2. Use the default test seller, or make another.
3. Square's sandbox card number is `4111 1111 1111 1111` with any future expiry and any CVC.

### Give the worker the values

Both providers' values go on `handsfreeos-worker` and nowhere else.

1. Open your password manager and put the Stripe client id on the clipboard.
2. In Terminal:

   ```bash
   fly secrets import --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

3. Type `STRIPE_CLIENT_ID=` then paste, with no space and no quotes. Press Return.
4. Do the same line by line for `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`, `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `SQUARE_APPLICATION_ID`, `SQUARE_APPLICATION_SECRET` and `SQUARE_WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_KEYS`.
5. Press Control-D when the last line is in.
6. Clear the clipboard:

   ```bash
   pbcopy < /dev/null
   ```

7. Check the names arrived:

   ```bash
   fly secrets list --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

You should see all seven in the `NAME` column. Fly never shows a value, only a digest. **Never run this import with `--app handsfreeos-api`** — the API refuses to start with any of these names present, and the deploy will fail.

`SQUARE_WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_KEYS` takes several keys separated by commas, so a signature key can be rotated without a gap: add the new one, save, then remove the old one a day later.

### Check it started

```bash
fly logs --app handsfreeos-worker
```

You should see the `worker started` line with `"payments":"real"`. If it says `"payments":"fake"`, neither application is configured; if the worker refuses to start, the message names the missing half (a Stripe client id with no secret key, or a Square application id with no secret).

### The watch items, and what to tell a client

These are the four that bite, and the one question to ask each client's bank.

- **Square signs you out every 30 days.** A Square seller's access token expires 30 days after it is granted. HandsFreeOS renews it every week on its own, and renews at once when a token has less than three days left — but a worker that has been down for a month cannot renew a token that has already lapsed. The business then sees **Reconnect** on the account in **Settings** → **Payments**, and nothing is taken until they press it. Stripe's access does not expire.
- **Square cancels a plan only at the end of its period.** Square has no "cancel now". A plan cancelled here keeps billing until the period the customer is in runs out, and they keep the visits they have paid for. HandsFreeOS says so on the button ("Cancel at the end of the period"), in the dialog and under the cycles, before anybody presses it. Stripe ends a plan immediately.
- **Stripe refuses an account another platform already controls.** Stripe lets only one platform manage a standard connected account at a time. A business whose accountant, website or old booking software already connected their Stripe account will see "That Stripe account is connected to another platform" with the three ways out: disconnect the other platform in their own Stripe dashboard, make a second Stripe account for HandsFreeOS, or connect Square instead.
- **A plan keeps billing after a disconnect.** Disconnecting an account destroys the sign-in here on purpose, and the provider goes on charging the customers whose plans live in it. So the disconnect asks first, lists the plans, and offers **Cancel them first** — which can only be done while the account is still connected. If they disconnect anyway, those plans are marked as no longer managed by HandsFreeOS and the plan page says how to end them at the provider.
- **Ask each client's bank whether bank transfer (ACH) is switched on.** It is the cheap rail and it leads on the customer's payment page, but neither provider turns it on for every seller by default — Stripe asks the business to enable ACH Direct Debit, and Square's bank transfers are not available to every merchant. If it is off, the account's own capabilities say so and HandsFreeOS simply doesn't offer it; the business should know that before they promise a customer they can pay by transfer. A transfer also takes one to three business days, and can be returned days later, which is why a deposit paid by transfer cannot hold a time the way a card can.

Two more things worth saying to a client in the same breath:

- **The money is theirs from the first payment.** Payouts go from Stripe or Square to their bank on the provider's own schedule. HandsFreeOS is never in the path, so there is nothing for them to chase us about and nothing of theirs for us to lose.
- **They can revoke us.** From their own Stripe or Square dashboard, without telling us. HandsFreeOS hears about it through the webhook, marks the account disconnected, and says so on the Payments page.

### Before a client takes a real payment

1. They connect their own account in **Settings** → **Payments**, signed in as an owner or admin. If they have more than one, mark the one money should land in as **Default**.
   - If people on the team are each paid into their own account (one person's automations work into one Stripe account, another's SEO work into a second), open **Who can use it** on each account and pick the people. **Only the people you pick** keeps an account to them; **Only the people you pick, and only this account for them** also stops them billing into the accounts open to everyone. Their invoices and plans then land in their own account without anyone choosing it, and **Money** can be split by the account things were paid into.
   - Only people who may send invoices are offered: owners and admins, and anyone an owner lets bill — for a role in **Settings** → **Permissions**, or for one person under **Members** (see [Who can do what](#who-can-do-what-roles-and-permissions)).
2. Fill in **Settings** → **Payments**: the business address that goes at the top of a document, the sales tax rate and what it is called, the estimate and invoice number prefixes and the number to start from, the payment terms, and the deposit they usually ask for.
3. Check the reminder ladder with them: three days before the due date, on the day, then three, seven and fourteen days after, each at 9 AM where the business is. Ask whether that is more or less than they would send by hand.
4. Add what they sell in **Settings** → **Products**, with the right tax setting on each. Anything collected for someone else — a permit, a licence fee — should be marked as not taxable.
5. If they take deposits at booking, turn it on per calendar in **Settings** → **Calendars** → **Payments**, and agree the share. Tell them a held time goes back on the calendar after fifteen minutes if nobody pays.
6. Send one real invoice for a small amount to a card they own, on the live account, and check it lands in their Stripe or Square balance and that the receipt reaches them.
7. Ask their bank question (above) before anybody promises a customer a bank transfer.
8. Tell them what HandsFreeOS will never do: it will not take a payment without a person raising the document, it will not chase a customer about money on its own — both money cards on Home end with a person reading the words and pressing send — and the AI teammate is never given a conversation about a bill.

### When something goes wrong

- **"Stripe isn't set up yet" or "Square isn't set up yet"** when a business presses Connect: the worker has no client id or application id for that provider. Check `fly secrets list --app handsfreeos-worker`.
- **The sign-in comes back and the account still says Pending:** the callback failed. `fly logs --app handsfreeos-worker` names the provider's own error code, and the account card in **Settings** → **Payments** shows the last error in plain words. A mismatched redirect URI is the usual cause — it must match Stripe Part 2 or Square Part 3 exactly.
- **"Some permissions were left unticked":** the seller unticked a permission on the provider's own screen. They press Connect again and accept all of them.
- **A payment succeeded at the provider but the invoice here still says unpaid:** a webhook did not arrive or did not verify. Check the provider's own webhook page for failed deliveries, and check the signing secret. Nothing is lost — both providers retry for days, and the payment lands the moment a delivery verifies.
- **A business says they were charged twice:** they weren't. A payment carries the customer's own press as its idempotency key, and a payment's status only ever moves forward, so a retried or doubled submit takes the money once. Show them **Money** → **Payments**, which lists every payment the business has taken, with what it was paid on, where it stands and which invoice it belongs to; the provider's own dashboard will show one charge against it.
- **"You can bill the customers you’re on. Ask an owner or admin to add you to this customer."**: the person may send invoices but isn't on that customer. Put them on it (the **Assigned** card on the customer), or have someone who manages money send it.
- **"That payment account is kept for other people on the team"** or **"None of this business's payment accounts is yours to bill into"**: the account was given to particular people under **Who can use it** in **Settings** → **Payments**, and the person billing isn't one of them. An owner adds them there, or opens the account to everyone again. Invoices the business sends by itself — automatic invoices, booking deposits, a plan's own cycles — are not held to this.
- **An account says Reconnect:** its token lapsed (Square) or the provider refused it. Nothing is taken until the business presses Reconnect and signs in again. Refunds on payments taken through the old sign-in still work once the same account is reconnected, because the credentials are found by the provider's account id rather than by the connection row.

## Usage balances: what businesses pay us

Every other money page in HandsFreeOS is about a business billing **its own** customers. This one is the other
direction: what the business pays **us** for the texts, calls, phone numbers and AI replies it uses on top of
its plan. Two different things, deliberately never sharing a page, a table or a card — the migration headers
say so, and somebody will eventually try to "unify" them.

The whole thing runs on two switches that are easy to confuse, so learn them first:

|                      | What it decides                                   | Where it lives                                                      |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `WALLET_MODE`        | Whether we **count** — `off`, `shadow` or `on`    | `[env]` in `apps/worker/fly.toml`, one setting for the whole server |
| A wallet's **stage** | Whether we **speak** — `off`, `warn` or `enforce` | On each business's own row, moved from `/admin` one at a time       |

Nothing a business sees or feels depends on `WALLET_MODE`. It depends on that business's stage, which starts
at `off` for everybody and only moves when somebody moves it. That is what makes the shadow week silent: the
ledger fills for a week, every balance goes deep into the negative because nobody has a card, and not one
business hears a word about it.

`WALLET_MODE` is **not a secret** — it goes in `fly.toml` beside `TELEPHONY_PROVIDER`, not in
`fly secrets import`. Putting it in the file means the current mode is visible in git and every change of it
is a one-line commit somebody reviewed.

The wallet needs migrations `20260930000700_usage_rate_card.sql` through `20260930001200_support_can_credit_a_balance.sql`. See "Apply new migrations".

**The AI's hearing and voice (Deepgram) is on the balance too, at 1.5×.** Three lines on the rate card: minutes
the AI listens on a live call (`speech.live.minute`), minutes of audio turned into words — talking out loud to
the Assistant or on a test call, and call and voicemail transcripts — (`speech.recording.minute`), and thousands
of characters the AI says out loud (`speech.voice.kchar`). One sentence costs a small fraction of a cent, so each
use is written to `app.speech_usage` and the worker's `speech.charge` job, every 15 minutes, bills each
business's running total once it's worth 25¢ or a day old: one statement line per kind, priced by the card and
rounded once. With `WALLET_MODE` off nothing is billed and the totals wait. A business whose balance has run out
(stage `enforce`) can't talk out loud any more, the same as the rest of the AI. Needs
`20261009000100_speech_is_counted_in_characters.sql` and `20261009000200_speech_on_the_wallet.sql`. Transcripts
made by Twilio (the fallback without a Deepgram key) are not on the balance.

### Part 0: The Stripe account the money lands in

Before any of the parts below, the money has to have somewhere to go. That somewhere is **HandsFreeOS's own
Stripe account** — the same one set up in "Money: Stripe and Square", used a second way.

**There is nothing new to sign up for.** The `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` already on the worker does two separate jobs:

| The job                                   | How the key is used                                   | Whose money |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| A business billing its own customers      | The key **plus** that business's connected account id | Theirs      |
| A business topping up its balance with us | The key **on its own**, no connected account          | Ours        |

That second line is this section. A top-up charge is made directly on the HandsFreeOS Stripe account, so it
lands in the HandsFreeOS balance and pays out to the HandsFreeOS bank account on Stripe's own schedule.

Three things follow from that, and all three surprise people:

- **Square cannot be used for top-ups.** Square's OAuth only ever gives access to _someone else's_ account,
  which is the wrong direction for taking our own money. A wallet whose card is a Square card cancels the
  top-up with "Square can't be used for top-ups" rather than failing it. In practice every wallet card is a
  Stripe card.
- **The top-up needs no webhook.** Stripe answers the charge in the same call, and the job writes down what it
  said. The `/webhooks/stripe` endpoint in "Money: Stripe and Square" is a **Connect** endpoint — it routes by
  the connected account an event happened in, and an event from our own account belongs to no connected
  account, so it is answered with a 200 and dropped. There is nothing to add there.
- **The test key stays out of production.** The worker refuses to start in production with an `sk_test_` key,
  because a test key would take nobody's money and look like it had.

#### What to check before the shadow week

1. Confirm the worker has all three Stripe values:

   ```bash
   fly secrets list --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

   You should see `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` and `STRIPE_CLIENT_ID`. The first two are what
   a top-up uses: the secret key makes the charge, the publishable key is what the card page sends the card
   details to from the browser. The client id is Connect's and is not used here.

2. Confirm the worker is on real payments:

   ```bash
   fly logs --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

   You should see `"payments":"real"` on the `worker started` line. On `"payments":"fake"` no card is ever
   charged, whatever `WALLET_MODE` says.

3. Check the HandsFreeOS Stripe account can actually pay out: **Settings** → **Business** → **Payouts** in the
   Stripe dashboard, with a bank account added and no outstanding verification. Charges succeed into a balance
   that cannot pay out, and the money sits there until somebody notices.

#### How a business puts a card on

Worth knowing, because it is the one part of this a business sees:

1. They open **Settings** → **Usage** and press to add a card.
2. The worker opens a card page. The card details go from their browser straight to Stripe — the same as
   everywhere else in HandsFreeOS, the number never reaches our database.
3. Stripe hands back a customer and a token for the card. Those, plus the brand, last four and expiry, are all
   that is written down. **Only the worker writes them**: the database refuses an update to any card column
   from a person's own session.
4. From then on, a balance under their floor charges that card for their top-up amount, without anybody
   pressing anything.

### Part 1: The shadow week

**This is the step that decides whether the price list is right, and it has to happen before a single customer
is charged.** The rate card was seeded from Twilio and Anthropic list prices; list prices are a guess until a
real week of a real business's traffic measures them. A guess that is wrong loses money quietly for a month.

1. Set the mode in `apps/worker/fly.toml`, in the `[env]` block:

   ```toml
   WALLET_MODE = "shadow"
   ```

2. Commit it and deploy the worker the usual way. Watch the log.

   ```bash
   fly logs --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

   You should see a `worker started` line. Nothing else changes: no card is touched, no warning is sent, and
   nothing stops. Every text, call, minute and AI reply now writes a row to `app.usage_ledger` with what it
   was priced from, and each night `wallet.reconcile` trues those rows up against each business's own Twilio
   subaccount.

3. Leave it for a week. A day is not enough — a rate key nobody used on Tuesday is a rate key you have not
   measured.

### Part 2: What to look at afterwards

1. **The margin, at `/admin/rates`.** The right-hand column is what we charged against what it cost us, per
   rate key, over the window. **Anything under 1.2× is the thing this week existed to find**: at 1.5× intended,
   a key that lands at 1.1× means the seeded cost is wrong, and it will go on being wrong until somebody looks.
2. **`/admin/health`.** Three rows matter here:
   - **Balances that disagree** — a cached balance that does not match its own ledger. This is the silent one:
     the balance is what every spending gate reads, so a drift means every gate is lying.
   - **Days not reconciled** — nights the true-up did not run for a business with a carrier account. A margin
     figure built on a missing day is not a measurement.
   - **Balances below zero** — expected in shadow, since nobody has topped up. Not a problem here; it is a
     problem later.
3. **One business, end to end, at `/admin/businesses/<id>`.** The balance block shows what they were charged
   beside what they cost us. Pick a busy one and read the statement.
4. **Against a real invoice.** Compare a week of `cost_30d_cents` for one business against the same week on
   Chris's actual Twilio bill. The daily reconciliation should already have closed most of the gap; what is
   left is what we are not pricing at all.

### Part 3: Fixing the card

Live rate rows are never edited. A correction is a **whole new version** of the card — the function takes
every row, not a patch, so a version is always a complete, readable price list:

```sql
select private.publish_usage_rates(
  '[{"key": "sms.outbound.segment", "unit": "segment", "cost_micros": 10900, "markup_bp": 15000}, …]'::jsonb,
  'Twilio raised the carrier fee on 3 Oct'
);
```

It refuses a set that does not cover every key the live card has, and it is staff-admin only
(`platform.rates.manage`). It returns the new version number. Every ledger row is stamped with the version
that priced it, so a mid-month change is honest — old rows still say what they were charged under and why.
`/admin/rates` shows the live card and the realised margin against it.

### Part 4: Switching a business on

One business at a time, from `/admin/businesses/<id>`. **Two steps, never one.**

1. **Move them to Warned.** They now see their balance, their statement and what things cost, and they are
   told — by email, by push and on Home — when the balance runs low or runs out. Nothing stops. This is the
   stretch where they put a card on. Watch what they actually do with it.
2. **Then move them to Stopped at zero**, once they have a card and have had the warnings. From that moment
   outgoing texts and calls stop when the balance is past its overdraft. **Calls coming in still reach them**,
   and incoming messages are still received and filed — that is a promise in terms §3, not a nicety.

Order: internal first, then a handful of friendly businesses, then everyone. The dialog asks why, and the
reason goes on the event, because a rollout is a series of decisions somebody should be able to explain a
month later.

There is deliberately **no global switch** for this. A global switch is how this gets turned on for a thousand
businesses by accident at two in the morning.

### Part 5: Turning it off

```toml
WALLET_MODE = "off"
```

Deploy. Counting stops immediately; nothing already recorded is lost, no balance is touched, and no business
is told anything. To stop a single business instead, move its stage back to Silent from `/admin` — that is the
faster and smaller answer to "this one business is having a bad time".

### When something goes wrong

- **A business says its texts stopped and it should not have:** check its stage at `/admin/businesses/<id>`.
  Only `enforce` stops anything. If it is on `enforce` and the balance is fine, look at "Balances that
  disagree" on `/admin/health` — a drifted cache is the one way a gate refuses a business that has money.
- **A business was warned during the shadow week:** it should be impossible; every channel checks the stage.
  If it happened, that business's stage is not `off`. Move it back and find out who moved it — the event says.
- **The margin looks impossible (very high, or infinite):** a rate key with charges but no cost. Usually the
  provider's daily records have not arrived for those days yet — they lag by about two. The other cause is a
  carrier charge we do not price at all; the reconciler will not invent a category for it, it logs a warning
  naming it. Search the worker log for `categories the rate card has never heard of`.
- **A card was charged twice:** it was not. The recharge row carries its idempotency key before the provider
  is called, the same key goes to Stripe, and a unique index allows one pending recharge per business. Show
  them their statement — a second charge would be a second `topup` row, and there will not be one.
- **A top-up was bigger than the business chose:** that is escalation, and it is deliberate. Several top-ups
  in a few days become one larger charge instead of many small ones, up to a cap shown on their own page. They
  were emailed before anything above twice their amount was charged. The fix they want is to raise their own
  top-up amount, which the email says.

## Founding seats

The founding offers are the first businesses on HandsFreeOS: twenty-five free seats, then a hundred at $497 paid
once, and partway through those the $97 monthly plan goes on sale beside them. The sequence moves on by itself —
the $497 seats open the moment the last free one goes — and the website follows it. Everything here happens
in **Admin** → **Founding**.

Founding needs the migrations `20261003000100_a_seat_at_the_founding_table.sql`,
`20261003000200_one_offer_opens_the_next.sql` and `20261003000500_paying_for_a_seat.sql`. See "Apply new
migrations".

### Approving somebody

1. Ask them to sign up to HandsFreeOS first, with the email they applied with. A seat belongs to a business, and
   there has to be one to give it to.
2. In **Admin** → **Founding**, find their application under **Waiting on you** and press **Approve**.
3. Paste their business id, add a note on why them if you like, and press **Approve and hold a seat**.
4. **Copy the claim link that appears, and email it to them straight away.** It is shown once. Only a scrambled
   copy is kept, so closing the window without copying it means approving them again.

You should see the seat under **Seats out**, marked "approved, not taken up". It is held for them for fourteen
days. A seat nobody takes up in that time goes back to the offer on its own, within the hour after it runs out.

### What they do with the link

They open it signed in as an owner or admin of the business the seat was approved for. Signed in as anybody
else, the page says so and offers to switch account — the link cannot put a seat on somebody else's business,
whoever holds it.

- **A free seat:** they press **Take up my seat**. Their workspace is on the founding plan at once, with its
  starting usage credit.
- **A $497 seat:** they press **Pay $497** and go to Stripe's own payment page. The seat turns on when Stripe
  tells us the money is in, not when they arrive back — so it needs the webhook in "Paying for a seat: the
  Stripe side" below. While they are paying, the seat stays held for them, and **Seats out** says "paying now".

### Paying for a seat: the Stripe side

The $497 is paid into HandsFreeOS's own Stripe account, the same one in "Money: Stripe and Square", through
Stripe Checkout. It needs the live secret key on the worker and **a second webhook endpoint**, separate from the
Connect one.

**Part 1: The secret key.** If the worker already has `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` from "Money: Stripe and Square" Part 3,
skip this. Otherwise copy the live secret key from **Developers** → **API keys** (it starts with `sk_live_`) and
put it on the worker the way that section's "Give the worker the values" does. The Connect client id is not
needed for this. **The worker refuses to start with a test key (`sk_test_…`) in production.**

**Part 2: The webhook for our own account.**

1. In the Stripe dashboard, in **live** mode, go to **Developers** → **Webhooks** (on newer dashboards,
   **Workbench** → **Webhooks**), and add a destination.
2. Choose **Your account**, not **Connected accounts**. These events happen in HandsFreeOS's own account; the
   Connect endpoint drops anything that isn't a business's.
3. Select these four events, and no others:
   - `checkout.session.completed`
   - `checkout.session.expired`
   - `checkout.session.async_payment_succeeded`
   - `checkout.session.async_payment_failed`
4. Set the API version to the one the worker pins (`API_VERSION` in `apps/worker/src/payments/stripe.ts`,
   today `2026-08-26.dahlia`).
5. Choose **Webhook endpoint**, and use this address:

   ```text
   https://hooks.handsfreeos.com/webhooks/stripe/platform
   ```

6. Create it, then press **Reveal** under **Signing secret** and copy it. It starts with `whsec_`. It is **not**
   the Connect endpoint's secret; each endpoint has its own.
7. Save it in your password manager as "Stripe — our own account", under webhook signing secret.
8. In Terminal:

   ```bash
   fly secrets import --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

9. Type `STRIPE_PLATFORM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=` then paste, with no space and no quotes. Press Return, then Control-D.

You should see `STRIPE_PLATFORM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` in `fly secrets list --app handsfreeos-worker`, and the worker
restart. Until it is there, pressing **Pay** tells the person that paying online isn't switched on yet and
keeps their seat held — the worker will not make a page nobody would hear back from.

### Paying for a seat: crediting the ad that brought them

The website's analytics (Opinly) sees where every visitor came from and who applied, but not the money: payment
happens in the app, and Opinly's script is kept out of the app because the app is full of other businesses'
customers. So when Stripe's event says a seat is paid, the worker reports a `purchase` of what Stripe took, keyed by
the checkout, with the email address the **application** was made with. Opinly matches that address to the visit
where it was typed, and credits the payment to the ad or post that brought them.

1. In Opinly, go to **Settings** → **Developers** and press **Create API key**. Copy it; it starts with `sk-` and
   is shown once. The `pk-` key in **Analytics** → **Setup** is the website's, not this one.
2. Save it in your password manager as "Opinly secret key".
3. In Terminal:

   ```bash
   fly secrets import --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

4. Type `OPINLY_API_KEY=` then paste, with no space and no quotes. Press Return, then Control-D.

Without it nothing is reported and nothing else changes. A paid seat then shows in Opinly's **Analytics** →
**Conversions** within a minute or so; one credited to **direct** means the person applied with an address the
website never saw them type (a seat staff gave out with no application, say).

### When a payment needs a person

- **Paid, but the seat could not be turned on.** Shown in red under the seat in **Admin** → **Founding**. The
  money is in and nothing was undone, but the seat was revoked while they were paying, or it ran out and went to
  somebody else. Either restore their seat (**Undo** under **Seats given back**, if there is room) and approve
  them again, or refund them in the Stripe dashboard: **Payments**, search for the `pi_…` in the worker log line
  `a founding seat was paid for and could not be turned on`.
- **"This is taking longer than it should" after paying.** Stripe's event has not arrived. Check the endpoint in
  Part 2 exists on **live**, and that the worker log does not say `rejected an unsigned or mis-signed Stripe
webhook for our own account`. A wrong secret is fixed by setting the right one; Stripe tries a failed event
  again for three days, so nothing is lost meanwhile.
- **Somebody paid twice.** They did not. One checkout is live per seat, and the same idempotency key goes to
  Stripe every time the page is asked for, so a second press of **Pay** opens the same page.

## A business's own web address

A business that has been going a while asks for this before it asks for anything else on this page: it wants
the links it sends and prints to read `go.lonestarhvac.com`, not `app.handsfreeos.com`. **Branded domains**
(M17) is that — one domain per business, on the pages its customers see and nowhere else.

What moves onto it: the public forms, payment links, estimate, invoice and plan links, the booking page,
change-or-cancel and waitlist links, the deposit-hold page, the chat window and the snippet that loads it.
**It is not a booking feature.** A business that takes no online bookings can have one: adding a domain names
the business's pages if nothing has yet (the same switched-off booking site row publishing a form makes), and
the domain keeps serving whether booking is on or off. With booking off, `/` on the domain says online booking
is off; everything else on it works as usual. What deliberately
does not: the app, sign-in, and the admin side. A HandsFreeOS sign-in form served on a customer's domain is a
phishing page built out of a feature, so `brandedRoute` (`packages/core/src/hosting/branded-paths.ts`)
redirects every one of those back to `app.handsfreeos.com`, and the names we reserve as booking-site slugs
(`app`, `admin`, `api`, `sign-in`, …) are reserved one level down too.

**Only the origin moves.** `https://go.lonestarhvac.com/i/AbCd1234EfGh567890` and
`https://app.handsfreeos.com/i/AbCd1234EfGh567890` are the same link, signed by the same key. So a text sent
last month keeps working after a domain is added, and keeps working after one is removed.

### What it needs

| Setting             | Required                        | Where                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `VERCEL_TOKEN`      | To offer branded domains at all | Vercel, **Account Settings** → **Tokens**. Scope it to the team that owns the web app project. Worker only, `fly secrets import`.                           |
| `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID` | With `VERCEL_TOKEN`             | The web app project's **Settings** → **General** → **Project ID** (starts `prj_`). The **web app** project, not the website.                                |
| `VERCEL_TEAM_ID`    | Only on a team account          | **Team Settings** → **General** → **Team ID** (starts `team_`). Leave unset on a personal account.                                                          |
| `SITE_HOST`         | No                              | `vercel`, `fake` or `off`. Defaults to `vercel` in production when there is a token and `off` when there is not; `fake` locally. Production refuses `fake`. |

**`off` is a real answer, not a missing one.** With no token the worker starts normally, the feature is simply
not offered, and every job that would call the host logs a line and stops. A business that adds a domain and
then waits forever for records nobody is fetching is worse off than one that was never offered it — so if you
do not want branded domains yet, leave the token unset rather than setting `SITE_HOST=off` and half-offering
them.

### Turn it on

1. In Vercel, open the **web app** project (the one serving `app.handsfreeos.com`), then
   **Settings** → **General**, and copy the **Project ID**.
2. **Account Settings** → **Tokens** → **Create**, scoped to that team. Copy it once; Vercel will not show it
   again. Put it in the password manager.
3. Give both to the worker:

   ```bash
   fly secrets import --app handsfreeos-worker <<'EOF'
   VERCEL_TOKEN=...
   VERCEL_PROJECT_ID=prj_...
   EOF
   ```

   `fly secrets import`, never `fly secrets set` — `set` puts the value in your shell history.

4. Wait for the restart, then check the worker's started line has `"siteHost":"vercel"`.

### What a business does

**Settings** → **Workspace** → **Your own web address**. It sits beside the business's name rather than
under Calendars, because one domain carries the forms, the payment links, the estimates and the invoices as
well as the booking page; the booking site page links across to it. No booking page has to be set up first.

1. They type the domain they want, usually a subdomain of one they already own
   (`go.lonestarhvac.com`). Ours is refused: nobody can point `handsfreeos.com` at themselves.
2. HandsFreeOS claims the name with Vercel and shows the records to add wherever their domain lives —
   their registrar, or whoever runs their website: a **CNAME**, which is what actually points the name
   here, and, when Vercel asks for one, a **TXT** that proves they hold the name before a certificate is
   issued for it.
3. They add what it shows. A job looks every 15 minutes, and **Check now** looks immediately. DNS commonly
   takes a few hours; the card says so rather than looking broken.
4. When the records are found _and_ the certificate has issued, the card says **Working** and every public
   link they are shown moves onto the new name within the minute.

**How many records there are is Vercel's answer, not ours.** A subdomain of a name the business already
runs usually verifies off the CNAME alone, so the common case is a **single** record and the TXT never
appears. Nothing in the card, the assistant's steps or this page promises a count before Vercel has given
one — a screen that says "two records" over one record is a screen a business stops trusting.

**The records arrive a moment after the domain does.** They are Vercel's to say, and the worker only asks
once `branded_domain.add` has returned, so the card has nothing to show for a second or two. It says it is
working that out, and fills itself in when the answer lands — a live update on the workspace channel, or
its own short poll if that channel is down. A card still saying it a minute later means the worker is not
draining the `branded_domain.check` job; look there, not at DNS.

**Verified is not working.** A domain whose DNS is right but whose certificate has not issued yet serves a
browser warning, which is worse than serving nothing — so `certificate_ready` is a separate column from the
status, and `private.site_for_domain` answers for neither until both are true. If you ever change this,
change nothing else first.

**Removing one is loud.** `branded_domain.remove` is risk 3, and the confirmation says why: the forms,
payment links, estimates, invoices and booking page go back to `app.handsfreeos.com` at once, and every QR
code, flyer and text already carrying that address stops working the moment it runs. Nobody can un-print the
flyers.

### Check one by hand

```bash
# What the business has to put in DNS, and where it has got to.
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "select domain, status, certificate_ready, last_error, next_check_at
                         from app.branded_domains order by created_at desc limit 20;"

# The records really there, from outside our network.
dig +short TXT   _handsfreeos.go.lonestarhvac.com
dig +short CNAME go.lonestarhvac.com

# Which business a host is, exactly as the web app asks.
curl -s https://hooks.handsfreeos.com/public/site-for-host/go.lonestarhvac.com

# End to end: their pages on their own name. `/` answers even with booking switched off.
curl -sI https://go.lonestarhvac.com/ | head -3
```

The last one is the check that matters, because it is the only one a customer would do.

### Good to know

- **Every call to Vercel is a job.** `branded_domain.check` runs on add and on **Check now**, reschedules
  itself every 15 minutes while a domain is unsettled, and stops once it is working.
  `branded_domains.sweep` looks at every domain daily, including the working ones — a business moves its DNS
  or lets a domain lapse, and otherwise the first anybody would know is a customer saying the link is broken.
- **A name Vercel says is taken is an answer, not a retry.** The card shows what the host said, the status
  goes `failed`, and the business either releases it at the other end or picks another name.
- **One domain per business.** Changing it is removing and adding, deliberately: a name that has been in
  somebody's DNS for a week is not something to silently repoint.
- **A name pointed at us that nobody set up gets a 404**, not one of our pages. The web app asks the worker
  which business a host is and serves nothing when the answer is nobody.
- **If the worker is unreachable**, the web app serves nothing on a branded domain rather than guessing, and
  every link builder falls back to `app.handsfreeos.com`. A confirmation text going out on the wrong name is
  a far smaller failure than one not going out at all.
- **Test it without a Vercel account.** `SITE_HOST=fake` decides from the name, the way the fake carrier
  decides from the last four digits: a name containing `taken` is refused, `slow` verifies but never gets a
  certificate, `missing` never finds the records, and anything else works on the second look.

## Moving a business here from another CRM

A business you take on is almost never starting from nothing. It has five years of customers, texts, calls, appointments and invoices in whatever it uses today, and it will not move until it believes none of that will be lost. **Migrations** is the part of HandsFreeOS that moves it, and the promise it makes is stricter than "the data is in there somewhere": the history has to feel as though the business had been using HandsFreeOS all along. A customer added in 2019 says 2019. A text sent on a Tuesday afternoon sits where a Tuesday afternoon belongs.

GoHighLevel is the first system we can read. Everything past the reading is source-neutral, so HubSpot, Jobber or Housecall Pro is a new adapter rather than a new migration platform.

Migrations need the migrations `20260923000100_migrations_core.sql` to `20260923000400_migrations_writes.sql`. See "Apply new migrations".

Without any of this, everything else in HandsFreeOS works. **Migrations** in the agency area simply says GoHighLevel is not set up.

### What it does, in order

1. **Connect.** Two ways in, and the screen offers both. Either the agency **signs into GoHighLevel** and approves the sub-accounts we may reach — read access only — or the business makes a **private integration token** in one sub-account and pastes it here with that sub-account's Location ID ("Connecting with a private token", below).
2. **Look.** Read-only, and safe to run again. It counts what is there, says how sure it is of each count, and writes down every place the old system holds something HandsFreeOS cannot hold the same way.
3. **Say where each one lands.** Every sub-account becomes a business here, or joins one you already have. Several may share one business; the page says what that mixes before anything moves.
4. **Choose and check.** Everything we can bring is ticked already. Untick what you do not want, read the plan, press the button.
5. **It arrives.** In small batches that can be paused, resumed and retried. Nothing goes out to a customer because of it: no text, no email, no invoice, no reminder.
6. **Check and finish.** Counts, duplicates, orphans and dates are all checked. Setup steps that are left — reconnect Stripe, change a DNS record, port a number — are listed as work to do, never as failures.

### What it will not do

- **It never touches the GoHighLevel account.** Nothing is changed there and nothing is cancelled. The business cancels when it is ready, and we tell them not to cancel a phone line before the carrier confirms the port.
- **It never rebuilds their automations.** HandsFreeOS answers, follows up, reminds and asks for reviews itself. We read their workflows to check nothing they rely on is missing, and recommend the setting that replaces each one.
- **It never brings websites or funnels.** Those are counted so the boundary is visible, and they keep working where they are.
- **It never copies a credential.** No payment keys, no OAuth tokens, no API keys. Anything that has to be live again is reconnected through the normal HandsFreeOS screens.

### Setting up the GoHighLevel app

1. Sign in at `https://marketplace.gohighlevel.com` as Go Biz Help and create a **marketplace app**.
2. Give it the read scopes the adapter asks for. The list is in `apps/worker/src/migrations/adapters/gohighlevel.ts` (`GHL_SCOPES`); it is read-only throughout.
3. Set the redirect URL to `https://hooks.handsfreeos.com/migrations/callback`. It names no source on purpose:
   GoHighLevel's marketplace form refuses a redirect URL containing "HighLevel", and the worker already knows
   which source a sign-in belongs to from its one-time state. The older `/migrations/gohighlevel/callback`
   still answers, so an app registered with it keeps working.
4. Copy the client id and client secret into your password manager.
5. On `handsfreeos-worker`, set `GOHIGHLEVEL_CLIENT_ID` and `GOHIGHLEVEL_CLIENT_SECRET`. Both, or neither — the worker refuses to start with one of them. Neither value goes in Vercel or GitHub.
6. `MIGRATION_SOURCE` picks itself: `real` in production or whenever a client id is set, `fake` otherwise. Production refuses `fake`. A server that will only ever take pasted private tokens has no client id to set, so set `MIGRATION_SOURCE=real` on it by hand.

### While the app is still waiting to be approved

GoHighLevel approves a marketplace app before anyone else can install it, but it lets **you** install your own unapproved app on your own sub-accounts first. That is what an app's version link is for — the address of the form
`https://app.gohighlevel.com/v2/location/<location id>/integration/<app id>/versions/<version id>`, which the marketplace gives you for the version you are testing. Open it while signed into that sub-account and install it there.

Two things have to be right before that install will come back to us:

- The app's redirect URL is already the worker's (`https://hooks.handsfreeos.com/migrations/callback`), and the worker has to be reachable at it. Until the domain is live, use whatever address the worker actually answers on and change it back afterwards — the redirect URL has to match exactly, character for character.
- The sub-account you install into is the one you will migrate from. An unapproved app reaches nothing else.

Until it is approved, that is the only way to sign in. The private token below is the way in that needs no app at all, and is worth using while approval is outstanding and for any client whose plan or agency will not add an app.

### Connecting with a private token

GoHighLevel calls these **private integrations**. One is made inside a single sub-account, its read access is ticked when it is made, and it works against the same API as a sign-in does.

What the business does, in their own GoHighLevel:

1. **Settings** → **Private Integrations** → create one. Call it HandsFreeOS.
2. Tick the **read** access for what they want brought across. "View Contacts" is the least it can usefully have; the full list the sign-in asks for is `GHL_SCOPES` in `apps/worker/src/migrations/adapters/gohighlevel.ts`, and it is read-only throughout. Nothing here ever writes to GoHighLevel.
3. Copy the token. It starts with `pit-` and is shown once.
4. Find the **Location ID**: **Settings** → **Business Profile**, or the long code in the address bar after `/location/`.

Then, in HandsFreeOS: **Migrations** → **Connect a CRM** → **Paste a private token**, and paste both. The token goes straight from that page to the worker — never through the API, and never into a link — and is sealed there before it touches the database, exactly like a sign-in's.

What is different about this door, and what to tell a business:

- **It reaches one sub-account.** GoHighLevel will not list an agency's locations for a private token, and will not hand out a per-sub-account token from one. An agency with twelve clients to move either signs in once, or pastes twelve tokens.
- **It never says what it was given.** A sign-in reports its scopes, so we can say "this sign-in cannot read calls" before reading anything. A private token reports nothing, so the scan finds out by asking, and a category that comes back refused is listed as refused with what to tick — never as an empty account.
- **It does not expire, and it cannot be refreshed.** If one stops working — usually because somebody deleted the private integration — the connection asks for a new one rather than trying to renew.
- **Deleting it ends our access completely.** After the move, the business deletes the private integration in GoHighLevel. That is the whole of it; there is nothing to revoke on our side.

### Before the first real migration

**The adapter has not been run against a live GoHighLevel agency from this repository.** Its endpoints, its token exchange and its location-token exchange follow HighLevel's published v2 API, and the whole thing is built to find out rather than to assume — it probes each category with a one-record read and reports what actually came back, and every field it did not understand is kept rather than dropped. That is not the same as having done it. Before the first client:

1. Connect a **test** GoHighLevel account, or a sub-account you own.
2. Run the scan and read the inventory. Counts that look wrong, or categories marked "the old system will not give it", are what you are looking for.
3. Bring it into a **throwaway** business here, not a client's.
4. Read the report, then take it back with **Take it back** and check the business is as it was.
5. Write down what the field coverage actually was, category by category. That list is the thing that decides which categories can be called ready.

### The stand-in, for local work

Locally and in tests, migrations read a stand-in agency instead of GoHighLevel: two sub-accounts of a fictional HVAC company, deliberately awkward. The same customer appears in both on one mobile number. Two different Dave Smiths have different numbers. One customer's email points at one person here and their phone at another. Companies are out of reach, so "we were not allowed to look" is exercised; custom fields are readable and have nowhere here to go, so the other kind of gap is exercised too. It lives in `apps/worker/src/migrations/adapters/fake.ts`, and nothing in it can reach a real account.

### When something goes wrong

- **"The old system needs signing in to again."** The token expired or was revoked. Connect it again from **Migrations**; the migration picks up where it stopped. For a private token there is nothing to renew: make a new private integration in GoHighLevel and paste it again.
- **"GoHighLevel would not let that token read this sub-account."** Either the Location ID is not that token's sub-account, or the private integration was made with no read access ticked. Both are fixed in GoHighLevel, and the same dialog takes another go without starting again.
- **A batch keeps failing.** `app.migration_errors` holds a sanitized reason per record, and **Try N again** requeues them. Records that already came across are not brought twice — the source identity sees to that.
- **A customer is waiting on a decision.** The engine never guesses between two people. Those sit in the review queue and the rest of the import carries on around them.
- **The counts do not add up.** A source that is still being used while it is read is normal, and the check says so rather than failing. A _duplicate_ is not normal: the identity check would fail, and that is worth stopping for.

## Support and the admin side

Everything above is about the businesses. This is about you: the tickets customers send in, and the screens
that tell you how HandsFreeOS itself is doing. It lives at `app.handsfreeos.com/admin`, in the same app, and
it does not exist for anyone who does not work here — a customer who guesses the address gets the 404 page.

Setting up the email side is [Postmark Part K](#postmark-part-k-support-email-with-no-mailbox-to-sign-into).

### Getting in the first time

`PLATFORM_OWNER_EMAILS` on the worker (Fly Part 5) names the people who are support admins whatever the
database says. The worker confirms them every time it starts, so:

- Set it to your own email address before you look for `/admin`.
- If you ever lose every admin — nobody left to invite anybody — restart the worker and you are one again.

Everyone else joins by invitation: **Support people** → **Invite someone**. They get a link that works once,
only for the address it was sent to, and only after they have a HandsFreeOS sign-in with that same address.

### What each role may do

|                                           | Agent | Lead | Admin |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----- | ---- | ----- |
| Answer tickets, leave internal notes      | Yes   | Yes  | Yes   |
| Look at a business, read-only             | Yes   | Yes  | Yes   |
| See every business in the directory       | Yes   | Yes  | Yes   |
| Assign tickets, keep the saved replies    |       | Yes  | Yes   |
| The health page                           |       | Yes  | Yes   |
| Answer ideas, merge them, take them down  | Yes   | Yes  | Yes   |
| Move ideas along the roadmap, What's new  |       | Yes  | Yes   |
| Invite, suspend and remove support people |       |      | Yes   |

Nobody changes their own role, and the last admin cannot be removed or demoted — the database refuses both,
the same way it refuses removing a business's last owner.

### The day

- **Tickets** is the queue. "Needs an answer" is the one that matters; the rest are there for looking things
  up. A reply goes out from `support@handsfreeos.com` and the customer's answer comes back to the same
  ticket, so nobody has to match anything up by hand.
- **Ask the AI for a draft** writes a suggested answer from the saved replies and from tickets like this one
  that were answered before. It never sends anything: a person edits it and presses send. If it had nothing
  solid to go on it says so, and what it writes is the questions to ask instead.
- **Saved replies** are the answers worth writing once. They are also what the AI reads before it drafts, so
  a good one there improves every draft after it.
- **Businesses** is the directory: who signed up, who works there, when they last did anything. Their actual
  data — customers, messages, money — is not readable from here.
  A support admin can also pick the model a business's AI teammate thinks with on calls, under **AI on their
  calls**: **Default** is the worker's `VOICE_MODEL`, or **Claude Haiku 4.5** for faster replies. It changes
  from the next call and the next test call, with no redeploy, so try it on your own business first.
- **Health** is what has failed lately across every business: jobs, webhooks, bounced email, failed texts,
  failed payments, and work still queued. Look here before a customer has to tell you.

### Looking at a business

A support person can open a business read-only to see what the customer sees, from the ticket or from the
business's page. It needs a reason, it ends by itself (15 minutes, an hour, or four), and:

- **Nothing can be changed while it is open.** The database gives no write rule to someone with no role in
  that business, and the API refuses every command outright.
- **The business is told.** Their own audit log gets an entry naming the person, the reason, and how long it
  lasted. That is deliberate: it is the thing that makes this safe to have.

The banner across the top says which business it is and how long is left. **Stop looking** ends it at once.

### Chat on handsfreeos.com

The website's chat button is the same widget a business puts on its own site, pointed at us. To turn it on:
