1. In HandsFreeOS, open a business you own (Go Biz Help's own workspace is the natural one), then
   **Settings** → **Website chat**, and set it up as a business would: who it is for, what it may say, and
   when a person takes over.
2. Copy its key — the `wk_…` part of the snippet it shows you.
3. In Vercel, on the **handsfreeos-site** project, add `NEXT_PUBLIC_CHAT_WIDGET_KEY` with that value, and
   redeploy.

With no key set the site simply has no chat button, and the support page's email address and the in-app
**Get help** still work. Nothing on the site breaks if the key is wrong: the widget answers 404 and the
button never appears.

### If support mail stops arriving

1. In Postmark, open the **HandsFreeOS Support** server's inbound stream → **Activity**. If nothing is there,
   the mail never reached Postmark: check the MX record on `handsfreeos.com`.
2. If Postmark shows it but no ticket appears, the webhook is failing. `fly logs --app handsfreeos-worker`
   will show it. A `403` means the webhook password is wrong; Postmark stops retrying after a `403`.
3. Mail to an address that is not in `SUPPORT_ADDRESSES` is accepted and dropped on purpose. Add the address
   there if it should open a ticket.
4. An out-of-office reply is dropped on purpose too, and says so in the worker's log.

## Ideas, the roadmap and What's new

The board where the people who use HandsFreeOS tell you what would make it better, vote on what matters to
them, and follow an idea from "under review" to "done" — the same thing GoHighLevel keeps at
ideas.gohighlevel.com, built into the app. It needs nothing set up: no new service, no new setting, and the
emails go out the way the team's other emails do (`SMTP_URL` and `MAIL_FROM` on the worker). The tables are
migration `20261006000100_ideas_and_whats_new.sql`, in the `platform` schema beside the support desk.

### What the businesses see

- **Ideas** is a place in every business's side menu, for every role, just above Settings (and under **More**
  in the suggested menu). It has three tabs: **Ideas** (the board), **Roadmap** (planned, being built, and
  shipped in the last ninety days) and **What's new**. A dot beside Ideas says What's new has something the
  person has not read yet.
- **Sharing an idea** asks for a title, a few words more and which part of HandsFreeOS it is about. While they
  type the title, the ideas already on the board that sound like it come up with a vote button, because a
  vote on the idea that exists counts for more than a second copy of it. Sharing an idea votes for it.
- **Voting, commenting and following.** One vote per person, taken back any time while the idea is open.
  Sharing, voting and commenting all follow an idea; **Email me updates** on its page turns that off.
- **What other businesses see of them** is a short name ("Dale R.") beside an idea or a comment they wrote,
  and nothing else: never their email, never their business, never what they voted for.
- **Limits.** Ten ideas a day and thirty comments an hour per person, so a script cannot fill the board. The
  database holds the line; the team is never counted.
- **On the phone** it is **Ideas** under **More**, with the same three tabs, sharing, voting, comments and
  **Email me updates**, and **New** beside it while What's new has something unread. None of it is kept on the
  phone, so with no signal each screen says it needs one; nothing waits in the queue of changes.

### The team's side

It is **Ideas** in `/admin` (see the role table above: every support role answers, leads and admins move).

- **The list** opens on **Under review**: the ideas nobody here has answered yet. Each row says how many
  different businesses voted for it, which is a better signal than the vote count alone, and who shared it
  from which business.
- **An idea's page** has everything a business sees, plus who shared it (name, address, business) and every
  voter with their business. From there:
  - **Where it stands** moves it: Under review, Planned, In progress, Done, Not planned. Write a note — it is
    shown on the idea and goes into the email — and leave **Email the people following it** ticked. With the
    status unchanged, a note alone posts an update ("still planned, now for spring").
  - **Answer as the team** posts a comment with the HandsFreeOS badge, and emails whoever shared the idea:
    ask your questions here.
  - **Is it a duplicate?** lists the ideas that sound like it; **Merge into** folds it into one of them. Its
    votes and followers move over (anybody who had turned the emails off stays off), it leaves the board, and
    its followers are told where it went.
  - **Take it off the board** is for spam and for things that are not ideas at all. Its author still sees it,
    with a line saying the team took it down.
- **What's new** is where you write what shipped. An entry is a draft only the team sees until you press
  **Publish**. Link it to the ideas it delivers: publishing marks them **Done** and emails everybody following
  them, with the entry's title in the email. **Unpublish** takes it back to a draft (ideas it marked Done stay
  Done); only a draft can be deleted.
- **Areas** (admins and leads) are the parts of HandsFreeOS an idea can be about. Add one when a part of the
  product ships; archive one to stop new ideas going into it (the ideas already there keep it).

### The emails

- **An idea moves** (a new status, a note, shipped in What's new, or merged into another): one email to
  everybody following it who still works in a business here, except whoever made the change. The subject says
  what happened ("“Send invoices by text” is planned") and the button opens the idea.
- **The team answers** in the comments: one email to whoever shared the idea, if they still follow it.
- **Nobody is told twice.** Each email is written down as it goes, so a retry after a failure carries on
  where it stopped.
- The link in an email is `app.handsfreeos.com/app/ideas/<id>`, which opens the idea in the business the
  person was last in (or on the admin side, for somebody who works here and in no business). On a phone with
  the app, the same link opens the idea in the app, in the business it had open last.

Locally, `pnpm db:seed` puts seven ideas from four businesses on the board, three What's new entries and a
draft. Sign in as `chris@gobizhelp.test` and open `/admin/ideas`; the emails land in Mailpit.

## Push notifications: Expo

The phone app gets notifications people can act on from the lock screen: a customer waiting on a reply, urgent Action Center items, approvals, bookings and changes on their appointments, things assigned to them, and, for those who turn it on, a customer paying. They go through **Expo's push service**, which is free and hands each one to Apple or Google. Push is a second channel beside the emails, and the emails don't change.

What lives where:

- **The worker** holds one value, `EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN`, and sends every push with it. The API refuses to start with any variable starting with `EXPO_`, apart from the phone app's public `EXPO_PUBLIC_` build settings.
- **EAS**, Expo's build service, holds Apple's push key and Firebase's service account for Android. They are set up with the app's builds, not here.
- **The database** holds each person's phones (`app.push_devices`) and their six switches (`users.settings.push`).

Without the token, everything else works. The worker starts, logs `EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN is not set: push notifications to phones are off until it is`, and its `worker started` line shows `"push":"none"`. Phones still register; they just get nothing.

Push needs the migrations `20260921000500_push.sql` and `20260921000700_mobile_grants.sql`. See "Apply new migrations".

### Before you start

- The Expo organization for Go Biz Help, the one the app's EAS builds use, with you as an owner.
- The worker already running (Fly Part 7).
- Your password manager, open.

### Expo Part 1: A robot user and its token

A robot user's token keeps working when a person leaves the organization, so the worker never depends on anyone's own account.

1. Sign in at expo.dev and switch to the Go Biz Help organization.
2. Open the organization's **Settings** → **Access tokens**.
3. Under **Robot users**, add a robot user named `handsfreeos-worker` with the **Developer** role.
4. Create an access token for it named `handsfreeos-worker push`, and copy it straight into your password manager as `EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN`. Expo shows it once.

You should see the robot user and its token in the list. If the screens have moved, search Expo's documentation for "robot users" and "access tokens".

### Expo Part 2: Give the worker the token

1. Put the token on the clipboard from your password manager.
2. In Terminal:

   ```bash
   fly secrets import --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

3. Type `EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN=` then paste, with no space and no quotes. Press Return, then Control-D.
4. Clear the clipboard:

   ```bash
   pbcopy < /dev/null
   ```

5. Watch the worker restart:

   ```bash
   fly logs --app handsfreeos-worker
   ```

You should see the `worker started` line with `"push":"expo"`. **Never import it with `--app handsfreeos-api`**: the API refuses to start with it.

### Expo Part 3: Turn on enhanced push security

With enhanced security on, Expo refuses any push that doesn't carry one of your access tokens, so a push token copied off a phone can't be used to send anything. Turn it on only after Part 2: from then on, a push without the token is refused.

1. In the same **Settings** → **Access tokens** page, turn on **Enhanced Security for Push Notifications**.
2. Trigger a push you can see: while you're signed in on the app, have a teammate assign a lead to you on the web.

You should see the notification on the phone within a few seconds, and no `Expo refused some pushes` line in `fly logs --app handsfreeos-worker`.

### Expo Part 4: The phone app's side

A phone only gets a push token from Expo once the app knows its Expo project, and Apple and Google only deliver once EAS holds their keys. Until then the app registers nothing: Settings → Notifications on the phone says **Not in this build**, and nothing is sent to it. Test builds (`EXPO_PUBLIC_E2E=1`) register a stand-in token instead, for the worker's stand-in (see "The push stand-in" in "Local development"). Do these parts when the app's first EAS builds start, with the Expo organization from "Before you start".

1. **The project id.** In Terminal, in `apps/mobile`, run `eas init` while signed in to the Go Biz Help organization, and let it create the project `handsfreeos`. It prints the project's id. The app keeps it in one place: `expo.extra.eas.projectId` in `apps/mobile/app.json`, empty until now. Because the app also has `app.config.ts`, `eas init` asks you to paste the id there yourself. Paste it between the quotes and commit.

   You should see, on a build made after the commit, Settings → Notifications → **This phone** say **On**, and the web's Settings → Account say **On 1 phone**.

2. **Apple's push key.** Run `eas credentials --platform ios`, choose the production profile, then **Push Notifications** → **Set up a push key**, and let EAS create the key in the Apple Developer account of Go Biz Help LLC (team `8246H5FJ42`), never a personal team. EAS keeps the key; it never goes in this repository or on Fly.

   You should see **Push key** with a key id under the iOS credentials. If Apple refuses because the account already has two push keys, choose **Use an existing key** and give EAS one you keep in your password manager as a `.p8`.

3. **Firebase for Android.** Android pushes go through Firebase Cloud Messaging.
   1. At console.firebase.google.com, create a project named `HandsFreeOS` (Analytics off), then **Add app** → Android, with the package `com.gobizhelp.handsfreeos`. Download `google-services.json` into `apps/mobile/`.
   2. In `apps/mobile/app.json`, under `expo.android`, add `"googleServicesFile": "./google-services.json"`, and commit both. The file holds the Firebase project's public client settings, not a secret.
   3. In Firebase, open **Project settings** → **Service accounts** → **Generate new private key**. It downloads a JSON key: that one is secret. Run `eas credentials --platform android`, choose the production profile, then **Google Service Account** → **Manage your Google Service Account Key for Push Notifications (FCM V1)** → **Set up** → upload the file. Then delete the downloaded file (move it to the Trash and empty it).

   You should see **FCM V1 service account key** set under the Android credentials.

4. **Time-sensitive notifications.** The urgent kinds are sent as time-sensitive, so they break through an iPhone's Focus. The app already asks for the `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.time-sensitive` entitlement in `app.json`, and EAS turns the capability on for the app's identifier when it builds.

   You should see, at developer.apple.com → **Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles** → **Identifiers** → `com.gobizhelp.handsfreeos`, **Time Sensitive Notifications** and **Push Notifications** ticked, and **Associated Domains** too (for links).

5. **Links' fingerprints.** Links in emails open the app on Android only once `assetlinks.json` names the app's signing certificates. See "Links that open the phone app".

6. **Try it on real phones.** Sign in on an iPhone and an Android phone from store or internal builds. Have a customer text the business number (or text it yourself from a phone that isn't on your team): the notification shows on both, with **Reply**, **Call** and **Let AI handle** when the AI teammate could take the conversation. Reply from the lock screen: the iPhone asks for Face ID first, the Android phone for its unlock. The customer gets exactly one text.

### What the buttons do

| Button                 | What happens                                                                          | Asks for the phone's unlock first |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Reply                  | Typed in the notification, sent as a text, email or chat message in that conversation | Yes                               |
| Call                   | Opens the app at the conversation or lead                                             | No (the app opens)                |
| Let AI handle          | Hands the conversation to the AI teammate                                             | Yes                               |
| Let HandsFreeOS handle | Hands the Home item to HandsFreeOS                                                    | Yes                               |
| Snooze 1 hour          | Snoozes the Home item for an hour from the press                                      | No                                |
| Approve                | Approves the AI teammate's draft or the workflow step                                 | Yes                               |
| Review, Open           | Opens the app on the page the notification is about                                   | No (the app opens)                |

A button pressed twice, or on two of the person's phones, does it once. What the button did replaces the notification: it goes away once done (a reply typed in an Android phone's notification shade stays, saying "Your reply was sent.", because Android keeps a notification someone replied to until they clear it); with no signal it says the change goes as soon as HandsFreeOS can be reached; a refusal says why, and a tap opens Changes on this phone; a reply in the business's quiet hours asks, when tapped, whether to send now or when quiet hours end. On an Android phone that is locked, a button that needs the unlock waits: the notification says "Unlock your phone to send your reply.", and tapping it opens the app, which asks for Face ID or a fingerprint, then sends. A reply that waited more than 30 minutes asks "Still send?" first.

### What people get

| Kind                          | When                                                                                                                                                                  | Who                                                     | Its switch           |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| A customer waiting on a reply | A customer's new text, email or website chat arrives and nobody has answered it yet. Not while the AI teammate has the conversation: people hear when it hands over   | The conversation's assignee, else the owners and admins | On unless turned off |
| Urgent items                  | A hot lead after 10 minutes, a new lead nobody answered after 15 open minutes, or a customer still waiting past the business's reply threshold, with the urgent email | The assignee, else the owners and admins                | On unless turned off |
| Approvals                     | An AI teammate draft or a workflow's approval step waits                                                                                                              | Whoever may decide it                                   | On unless turned off |
| Your appointments             | Booked, moved, cancelled or given to someone                                                                                                                          | The people working it                                   | On unless turned off |
| Assigned to you               | A lead, a conversation, a task or a Home item                                                                                                                         | The new assignee                                        | On unless turned off |
| A customer pays               | An invoice is paid in full                                                                                                                                            | The owners and admins, and whoever the invoice is on    | Off until turned on  |

Each person sets these beside their email switches, on the web (Settings → Account) or in the app (Settings → Notifications): they're the same switches. Whoever did something never gets a push about it. A conversation has one notification on a phone: several messages within 2 minutes update it without buzzing again, and the urgent push for a customer still waiting takes its place. A push goes to every phone the person is signed in on, once: a retried job never sends it twice. `apps/worker/src/push/README.md` is the full contract the app is built on, with every button and what it does.

### Phones that are gone

About 15 minutes after each push, the worker asks Expo what Apple and Google said. A phone the app was removed from (`DeviceNotRegistered`) is turned off, unless the app registered it again since, and gets nothing more until the person opens the app on it again. Signing out, or turning notifications off on a phone, turns it off at once.

### When something goes wrong with push

- **Nobody gets pushes, and the worker's log says `push is off`:** it has no `EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN`. Do Expo Part 2.
- **The log says `Expo refused some pushes` or `Apple or Google refused some pushes` with `InvalidCredentials`:** the token was revoked or mistyped, or Apple's or Firebase's credentials in EAS are missing or expired. Make a new token (Expo Part 1, step 4) and import it again, and check the app's push credentials with `eas credentials`.
- **One person gets nothing:** check their switch for that kind, that they're signed in on the phone, and that the phone itself allows HandsFreeOS notifications. A phone Expo reported gone stays off until the app opens on it again.
- **A push never came while the phone was off:** Apple and Google keep trying for 12 hours for a customer's message and the urgent kinds, and a day for the rest. The emails still went.

### Rotating the token

1. Create a new token for the robot user (Expo Part 1, step 4).
2. Import it on the worker (Expo Part 2). The worker restarts with it.
3. Revoke the old token in Expo.

## The phone app: builds and the stores

The phone app is built by **EAS**, Expo's build service, never on your Mac. A build is made from a commit, carries the addresses of HandsFreeOS's servers baked into it, and goes to TestFlight or to Play's internal testing track. Nothing here is public until you promote it.

This section is about the hosted side: the settings a build carries, how to make one by hand, how a commit on `main` makes one by itself (Phone Part 4), and what goes wrong. The store listings themselves — the text, icons, screenshots, privacy answers, age rating and the demo business a reviewer signs into — live in `apps/mobile/store/`, with [`release-checklist.md`](../apps/mobile/store/release-checklist.md) as their running order. Push credentials are in "Push notifications: Expo".

### Before you start

You need:

- The Expo organization for Go Biz Help, with you signed in. `eas-cli` isn't installed in this repository, so every command below runs through `npx`, which fetches it:

  ```bash
  npx --yes eas-cli@latest whoami
  ```

  You should see `gobizhelp`.

- The API, the web app and the sync service already live, because a build points at them: Fly Parts 1 to 10, "The web app on Vercel", and Sync Parts 1 to 9. A build made before the sync service exists opens and signs in, then shows nothing — the phone reads every record from its own copy, which only the sync service fills.
- The Apple and Google developer accounts, and the rest of what [`release-checklist.md`](../apps/mobile/store/release-checklist.md) lists.

### What a build carries: the `EXPO_PUBLIC_` settings

Metro, which packages the app, replaces every `process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_…` it can see with the value that was set **when the build ran**, and writes the result into the bundle. There is no configuration file on the phone and nothing is fetched at startup: a build points where it pointed the day it was made, for good.

| Name                                   | Required       | What it is                                                                   | Its value                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`             | Yes            | Supabase, for signing in                                                     | `https://ybupfghakoszfcxhyrby.supabase.co`                                |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` | Yes            | That project's publishable key                                               | The `sb_publishable_…` key from the Supabase dashboard                    |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL`                  | Yes            | The API, which every change the phone makes goes to                          | `https://api.handsfreeos.com`                                             |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_SYNC_URL`                 | Yes            | The sync service, which fills the phone's copy                               | `https://sync.handsfreeos.com`                                            |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_WEB_URL`                  | No, but set it | The web app, for the pages the phone links out to                            | `https://app.handsfreeos.com` (also the default)                          |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_WORKER_URL`               | No, but set it | The worker: **the Assistant**, and test builds' stand-in push routes         | `https://hooks.handsfreeos.com`                                           |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_MATOMO_SITE_ID`           | No, but set it | Matomo's id for the phone app, which counts screens (`src/lib/analytics.ts`) | `4`, the phone app's site in gobizhelp.matomo.cloud; unset counts nothing |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_PASSKEYS_ENABLED`         | No             | Shows passkey sign-in                                                        | Leave unset until passkeys work                                           |
| `EXPO_PUBLIC_E2E`                      | No             | Builds for the Maestro flows                                                 | Leave unset                                                               |

The first four are the ones `isConfigured()` checks (`apps/mobile/src/lib/config.ts`). With any one of them empty the app opens on **"This build isn't connected"** and goes no further. Every one of these ends up readable inside the app on anyone's phone, so a secret must never be among them — that is what `EXPO_PUBLIC_` means.

`EXPO_PUBLIC_WORKER_URL` is not checked by `isConfigured()`, so a build without it starts and works — except that **Ask HandsFreeOS says "The Assistant can't be reached from this app"**, because the Assistant streams from the worker rather than the API (`apps/mobile/src/assistant/stream.ts`). It used to be described here as a test-build-only setting; that was wrong, and a build made on that advice has no Assistant. Set it for `production` and `preview` along with the other five.

**They live in EAS, not in this repository.** `apps/mobile/.env.local` is for your Mac and is git-ignored, and EAS leaves git-ignored files out of what it uploads. Local values therefore cannot reach a build, by design. Each profile in `eas.json` names the EAS environment it reads with `"environment"`: `production` and `preview` both point at the live servers; `development` is for builds that talk to your Mac.

### Phone Part 1: Put the six settings in EAS

Do this once. They stay until you change them, and every later build picks them up.

1. Check what is there now, from `apps/mobile`:

   ```bash
   npx --yes eas-cli@latest env:list production
   ```

   An empty list is what caused the "This build isn't connected" screen the first time. Note that `env:create` is deprecated and that `env:set` has no `--force`: it creates or updates either way.

2. Set each one, in both environments at once. Repeat this for all six names in the table, changing `--name` and `--value`:

   ```bash
   npx --yes eas-cli@latest env:set --scope project --name EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL --value "https://api.handsfreeos.com" --type string --visibility plaintext --environment production --environment preview --non-interactive
   ```

   You should see `✔ Created variable … on project @gobizhelp/handsfreeos.` each time.

3. Read them back:

   ```bash
   npx --yes eas-cli@latest env:list production
   ```

   You should see all five, with the values from the table.

`--visibility plaintext` is right for all of them: they are public by nature, and it is the only visibility EAS will also show you afterwards. Never set one to `secret` — the build can still read it, but you never can, and these are values you will want to check.

### Phone Part 2: Make a build

1. **Change into the app's own folder.** This matters more than it looks:

   ```bash
   cd ~/Projects/HandsFreeOS/apps/mobile
   ```

   Run `eas build` from the repository root instead and it does not fail — it decides the root is an unconfigured Expo app, writes a stub `eas.json` and `app.json` there, asks you for a bundle identifier, and only then stops on a missing `expo` package. Delete both files if that happens; neither belongs in the repository, and a later build that found them would use them.

   Check too that you are not in `~/Projects/HandsFreeOS-build` or another worktree. `git worktree list` shows them, and one of them sits in detached HEAD on an old commit.

2. Commit everything first. `eas build` uploads your working tree, uncommitted changes included, so a build is only a commit you can find again if the tree is clean. `eas.json` no longer enforces this with `requireCommit`: EAS's own dependency install rewrites `pnpm-lock.yaml` on its machines, and with `requireCommit` on, every workflow update and build stopped on that "dirty" tree.

3. Build, and send it on in the same step:

   ```bash
   npx --yes eas-cli@latest build --profile production --platform ios --auto-submit
   ```

   You should see, early in the output and before the build is queued:

   `Environment variables with visibility "Plain text" and "Sensitive" loaded from the "production" environment on EAS: EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL, EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY, EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, EXPO_PUBLIC_SYNC_URL, EXPO_PUBLIC_WEB_URL.`

   **Read that line every time.** It is the only place a build tells you what it is about to bake in, and a missing name here is the "This build isn't connected" screen twenty minutes later. A build takes roughly seven minutes.

4. For Android, the same with `--platform android`. It produces an `.aab` for Play's internal testing track. `--auto-submit` only works there once a Play service-account key exists; without one, upload the `.aab` by hand under **Testing → Internal testing → Create new release** (see [`release-checklist.md`](../apps/mobile/store/release-checklist.md), item 6).

EAS keeps the build number itself — `appVersionSource` is `remote` and both profiles set `autoIncrement` — so nothing in `app.json` needs touching between builds. `version` (`1.0.0`) is the one a customer sees and the one you edit by hand.

### Phone Part 3: Builds started from GitHub

Optional, and only worth it if you would rather not build from your Mac. EAS can build from a commit on GitHub instead.

1. Open the project's GitHub settings: `https://expo.dev/accounts/gobizhelp/projects/handsfreeos/github`.
2. Install the Expo GitHub App, then link `gobizhelp/handsfreeos`. You need Owner or Admin on the Expo account.
3. Set **Base directory** to `apps/mobile`. Without it the build looks for the app in the repository root and finds a monorepo.

Each profile you build this way also needs an `image` in `eas.json` — `preview` and `production` have `"image": "latest"` for both platforms. Leave it out and there is no error message: the build simply never dispatches.

A GitHub build reads the commit **as GitHub has it**, so push first. It is an easy way to build yesterday's code by accident.

### Phone Part 4: Releases that happen by themselves

Parts 2 and 3 are a person typing `eas build`. This part is the Vercel arrangement for the phone: a commit lands, and the right thing ships without anybody starting it. Three files in `apps/mobile/.eas/workflows/` describe it — beside `eas.json`, which is where EAS looks for them — and one GitHub workflow starts the production one.

| When                             | What runs                                                          | What reaches a phone                                                                                        | How long                       |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| A push to any branch but `main`  | `preview-update.yml`                                               | An over-the-air update on an EAS branch of the same name, for development and preview builds                | About a minute                 |
| The `mobile-build` label on a PR | `preview-build.yml`                                                | An installable build for both phones, linked from the pull request                                          | About seven minutes a platform |
| CI goes green on `main`          | `deploy-production.yml` via `.github/workflows/mobile-release.yml` | Either a build on TestFlight and Play internal testing, or an over-the-air update to the production channel | A minute, or half an hour      |

**The part that makes this work is the fingerprint.** `app.json` sets `runtimeVersion` to `{ "policy": "fingerprint" }`, which hashes everything native about the app — each native module, each config plugin, each setting in `app.json` and `app.config.ts` that reaches the built app. The production workflow takes that hash and asks EAS whether a production build already carries it. If one does, the commit changed JavaScript only, so it publishes an update and the phones holding that build pick it up on their next launch. If none does, the native side moved, so it builds and submits. Nobody decides this; the hash does, per platform, so iOS can take an update on the same commit that makes Android build.

This is also the rule that keeps an update honest: a phone is only ever offered an update whose fingerprint matches the build it is running. JavaScript written against a native module that build doesn't have is never handed to it.

**A build on EAS is not a build on the phones.** The question the workflow asks is whether a build with the fingerprint exists, not whether it reached TestFlight. A run that builds and then fails, at the submission or anywhere after, leaves its build on EAS, and without a guard every later run would take it as shipped and send updates only it can run. That happened on 23–24 September: TestFlight build 9 got none of a day's updates and kept closing on a bug fixed the night before. So `mobile-release.yml` first looks at the newest release that asked EAS to ship something; if that one didn't finish, it passes `rebuild`, and `deploy-production.yml` builds and submits both phones again (and still publishes the update). Releases that never asked EAS for anything — skipped, or cancelled while they waited their turn — are passed over.

#### What you need once

1. **Over-the-air updates turned on.** Done: `app.json` has `expo.updates.url` pointing at `https://u.expo.dev/22b0e923-de8b-4b67-9089-2c4bd440a956`, which is this project's id. Nothing else is needed, and `eas update:configure` does not have to be run. Adding it changed the fingerprint, so the first build after it is a new one on both phones — expected, and it only happens once.

2. **The Expo GitHub App on the repository.** Everything above hangs off this: EAS hears about a push, a pull request or a label only through it. Open `https://expo.dev/accounts/gobizhelp/projects/handsfreeos/github`, install the app, link `gobizhelp/handsfreeos`, and set **Base directory** to `apps/mobile`. Without the base directory EAS looks for the app at the repository root and finds a monorepo. This is the same link Phone Part 3 asks for; doing it once covers both.

3. **`EXPO_TOKEN` as a repository secret.** GitHub → **Settings** → **Secrets and variables** → **Actions** → **New repository secret**, named `EXPO_TOKEN`. Use an access token for the robot user from Expo Part 1, not a personal one: it can be revoked without touching anyone's account. Until the secret exists `mobile-release.yml` notes that it skipped and passes, so `main` stays green.

   The worker's `EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN` is a different token for a different job — pushes, and only pushes. Don't reuse either one for the other; revoking one should never silence the other.

4. **`MOBILE_SUBMIT_ANDROID`, once Play is ready.** A repository _variable_ (same page, **Variables** tab), set to `true`. Leave it unset until Play Console has an app record for `com.gobizhelp.handsfreeos` and EAS holds a Google service-account key (`eas credentials --platform android` → **Google Service Account** → **Manage your Google Service Account Key for Play Store submissions**). Until then the production workflow still builds the `.aab` and says, in its own log, to upload it under **Testing → Internal testing → Create new release**. iOS needs no such switch: TestFlight submission already works.

   `eas.json` no longer names `serviceAccountKeyPath`. It used to point at `../../secrets/play-service-account.json`, a file on a Mac that no build machine can read; EAS uses the key it holds for the project instead, which is the only kind a submission started by a workflow can use.

#### Reviewing a change on a phone

A preview update is the phone's version of a Vercel preview URL, with one difference worth remembering: it doesn't install anything. It replaces the JavaScript inside a development or preview build somebody already has. Open **Updates** in the build's own menu and the branch is listed there; the EAS dashboard has a QR code for the same thing.

When the app doesn't offer the branch, that is the fingerprint saying the native side changed. Add the `mobile-build` label to the pull request and an installable build for both phones is made and linked in a comment. It is behind a label because a build costs about seven minutes of EAS build time per platform and most pull requests don't need one.

iOS internal-distribution builds install only on phones registered to the Apple team. Register one with `npx --yes eas-cli@latest device:create` from `apps/mobile`; after that its builds install by tapping the link.

#### What production does, and what it still won't do

`mobile-release.yml` waits for CI on `workflow_run`, using the commit CI verified rather than whatever `main` points at by then, and then asks EAS to run `deploy-production.yml` on that commit through the workflows REST API. It waits up to forty-five minutes so a failure turns the job red next to the commit that caused it. A run that outlives the wait is not failed; it carries on at EAS, and the job prints its link.

The reach of all this ends at **TestFlight and Play's internal testing track**. Promoting a build to the public App Store or to a Play production release is still somebody opening a console and deciding to — which is what `release-checklist.md` means by "publishing still waits for Chris's go-live". Neither promotion is another upload: in App Store Connect you submit a TestFlight build for review, and in Play Console you promote the internal testing release.

One thing to be clear-eyed about: an over-the-air update to `production` reaches TestFlight testers, and later real customers, without store review. Both stores allow this for JavaScript, and it is why a fix can ship in a minute instead of a day. It also means `main` is the release branch in a way it is not for the API, where a bad deploy is one `flyctl` rollback away. If a staged rollout is ever wanted, the `update` jobs take a `rollout_percentage`, and `eas update:rollout` raises it afterwards.

### When something goes wrong with a build

- **The app opens on "This build isn't connected":** one of the first four settings was empty when the build ran. `npx --yes eas-cli@latest env:list production` shows what EAS holds now; fix it and build again. The build on the phone cannot be repaired — the values are inside it.
- **It signs in, but every screen is empty:** the app is connected but the sync service isn't answering. Check `curl -fsS https://sync.handsfreeos.com/probes/liveness` and "When the sync service needs attention".
- **`eas build` asks for a bundle identifier, or says "EAS project not configured":** you are in the wrong folder. See Phone Part 2, step 1, and delete any `eas.json` or `app.json` it wrote where it shouldn't have.
- **A GitHub build never starts:** the profile has no `image`, the base directory isn't `apps/mobile`, or the commit isn't pushed.
- **An EAS job fails with `Your repository working tree is dirty` and names `pnpm-lock.yaml`:** `requireCommit` is back on in `eas.json`. EAS's dependency install rewrites the lockfile on its machines, so every workflow update and build trips it. Take `requireCommit` out again.
- **Settings → Notifications on the phone says "Not in this build":** that is push, not these settings. See "Push notifications: Expo", Part 4.
- **`workflow:run` says `Failed to read workflow file` / `ENOENT`:** the path is wrong for where you are. The workflows live beside `eas.json`, so from `apps/mobile` the path is `.eas/workflows/deploy-production.yml`, and from the repository root it is `apps/mobile/.eas/workflows/deploy-production.yml`. A `.eas` folder at the repository root is never read: EAS looks under the GitHub App's base directory, which is `apps/mobile`.
- **Nothing happens on a push, a pull request or a label:** EAS never heard about it. The Expo GitHub App isn't installed on `gobizhelp/handsfreeos`, or its base directory isn't `apps/mobile`. Phone Part 4, step 2.
- **`mobile-release.yml` says `EXPO_TOKEN is not set`:** the repository secret is missing. Phone Part 4, step 3. The job passes anyway on purpose, so `main` stays green before Expo's robot user exists.
- **Testers' phones keep running old JavaScript although updates publish:** the updates are going to a build that isn't on the phones. On the phone, a crash's JavaScript stack names `main.jsbundle` from the build machine rather than an update. On the EAS website, **Builds** → the iOS build testers have → **Runtime version** differs from the runtime version of the latest update under **Updates** → `production`. The release that made the newer build failed after building it, so it never reached TestFlight. The next release after a failed one rebuilds by itself; to do it now, run **Phone app release** by hand under GitHub **Actions** with **rebuild** ticked (or `npx --yes eas-cli@latest build --platform ios --profile production --auto-submit` from `apps/mobile`, committed and pushed first). A release that outlived its 45-minute wait counts as finished even if EAS failed it later, so that one needs the hand run too.
- **The production run builds every time, even for a one-line JavaScript change:** the fingerprint isn't matching. Usually the `fingerprint` job and the `production` build profile are reading different environments, so they hash different `EXPO_PUBLIC_` values — both must say `production`. Uncommitted native changes in a build from your Mac do it too, so commit before building.
- **An update fails with `Web Bundling failed` and `Unable to resolve module @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm`:** something bundled the app for web. `app.json` sets `platforms` to `["ios", "android"]` so `eas update` without `--platform` (as in `preview-update.yml`) skips web; op-sqlite's web build needs a package the app doesn't have. Put `platforms` back if it is gone.
- **The app doesn't offer a branch's preview update:** the native side changed on that branch, so its fingerprint no longer matches the build in your hand. That is the guard working. Label the pull request `mobile-build` for an installable build.
- **An update published, but the app opens on "This build isn't connected":** the `update` job ran without `environment:`, so the bundle was built with no `EXPO_PUBLIC_` values. Both update jobs name their environment; if one is ever added, it must too.
- **The Android submission fails and nothing else does:** EAS has no Google service-account key for Play submissions, or Play Console has no app record yet. Unset the `MOBILE_SUBMIT_ANDROID` repository variable until both exist; the `.aab` is still built and waits in EAS.
- **The Android submission fails with `Google Api Error: Invalid request - The caller does not have permission`:** Google accepted the key EAS sent, but the service account it belongs to has no access to this app in Play Console. The repository isn't the cause: `eas.json` and `app.json` already give the right package, the internal track and a draft release. In Play Console, **Users and permissions** must list the service account as **Active** (the next item covers **Invite sent**), under exactly the key's `client_email`, which ends in `.iam.gserviceaccount.com` — `npx --yes eas-cli@latest credentials --platform android` prints the one EAS holds as **Client Email**. Its **App permissions** must include HandsFreeOS with **View app information (read-only)**, **Edit and delete draft apps**, **Release apps to testing tracks**, **Manage testing tracks and edit tester lists**, **Release to production, exclude devices, and use Play App Signing** and **Manage store presence** — the set in Expo's guide, `https://github.com/expo/fyi/blob/main/creating-google-service-account.md`. **Admin** is not needed. Access given a moment ago can take a day or more to reach Google's API. Then send the same build again from `apps/mobile`, without rebuilding: `npx --yes eas-cli@latest submit --platform android --profile production --latest`.
- **Play Console lists the service account as "Invite sent", not "Active":** a service account has no inbox and never signs in, so it can't accept an invite, and Play should list it as **Active** as soon as it is invited. **Invite sent** means Play is waiting for a person to accept, which points at the address: most likely it isn't exactly the key's `client_email` — a typo, or another account's address. There is nothing to accept and no email to wait for. Remove that invite, choose **Invite new users** again with `client_email` pasted from the key, give it HandsFreeOS and the permissions in the item above under **App permissions**, and save.

## Local development

This section runs all of HandsFreeOS on your Mac: the web app, the API, the worker, and a private copy of Supabase in Docker. It never touches the hosted Supabase project. By default nothing reaches Twilio, Postmark, Microsoft or Google either. The worker uses stand-ins for all of them, so nothing costs money and no phone is needed. The last part of this section explains how to swap one stand-in for the real provider when you need to.

Run every command in Terminal from the repository folder unless a step says otherwise:

```bash
cd ~/Projects/HandsFreeOS
```

### What you need first

You need Homebrew, Node 22 (22.12 or later), pnpm 12, Docker and the Supabase CLI. Check each one and install only what is missing.

1. Check Homebrew.

   ```bash
   brew --version
   ```

   You should see a line that starts with `Homebrew`. If you see `command not found`, install Homebrew from `https://brew.sh` and run the lines it prints under **Next steps**.

2. Check Node.

   ```bash
   node --version
   ```

   You should see `v22.12.0` or a later `v22` version. The repository asks for Node 22 in `.nvmrc` and for 22.12 or later in `package.json`. If Node is missing or older, install it:

   ```bash
   brew install node@22
   ```

   If Homebrew then prints lines that add Node to your PATH, run them and open a new Terminal window. In the new window, go back to the repository folder:

   ```bash
   cd ~/Projects/HandsFreeOS
   ```

   Then check again:

   ```bash
   node --version
   ```

   You should see `v22.12.0` or a later `v22` version.

3. Check pnpm.

   ```bash
   pnpm --version
   ```

   You should see `12.3.4` or another `12.x` version. The repository pins pnpm 12.3.4 in `package.json`. If you see `command not found`, install it:

   ```bash
   brew install pnpm
   ```

   If you see an older version, update it and run the check again:

   ```bash
   brew upgrade pnpm
   ```

4. Check the Supabase CLI.

   ```bash
   supabase --version
   ```

   You should see `2.117.0` or later. That is the version CI uses. If you see `command not found`, install it:

   ```bash
   brew install supabase/tap/supabase
   ```

   An older CLI may reject `supabase/config.toml`. If your version is older, update it:

   ```bash
   brew upgrade supabase
   ```

5. Install Colima and the Docker command-line tool. If you prefer Docker Desktop, download it from `https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/`, open it, and wait until it shows that it is running. Then skip this step and the next two.

   ```bash
   brew install colima docker
   ```

6. Start Colima with 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory.

   ```bash
   colima start --cpu 4 --memory 8
   ```

7. Check Colima.

   ```bash
   colima status
   ```

   You should see a line that contains `colima is running`.

Good to know about Docker:

- Colima does not start on its own after your Mac restarts. Start it before you start Supabase. It reuses the CPU and memory settings from the first start.

  ```bash
  colima start
  ```

- The `pnpm supabase:*` scripts and `pnpm env:local` find Colima's socket (`~/.colima/default/docker.sock`) for you. If you ever run `supabase` directly instead of through `pnpm`, tell it where Docker is first:

  ```bash
  export DOCKER_HOST="unix://$HOME/.colima/default/docker.sock"
  ```

### First-time setup

Do these once, in order.

1. Install the project's dependencies.

   ```bash
   pnpm install
   ```

   You should see pnpm finish without errors.

2. Start the local Supabase stack: Postgres, Auth, Realtime, Storage, Studio and Mailpit.

   ```bash
   pnpm supabase:start
   ```

   The first run downloads the Docker images and can take several minutes. If the two private files below do not exist yet, it also creates them and prints one line for each. If they already exist, it leaves them alone and prints nothing about them. Git ignores both.
   - `.env` at the repository root, copied from `.env.example`. It prints `Created .env from .env.example (Google OAuth values stay empty until you fill them in).` Only the Supabase CLI reads this file, for the optional Google sign-in described later in this section.
   - `supabase/signing_keys.json`, the key the local stack signs sign-in tokens with. It prints `Generating a local ES256 signing key: supabase/signing_keys.json (gitignored).` Never share or commit this file.

   You should see a summary of local addresses and keys when it finishes. You do not need to copy anything from it; the next step does that.

3. Write the local settings files.

   ```bash
   pnpm env:local
   ```

   You should see four lines: `wrote .env.local (11 vars)`, `wrote apps/api/.env (6 vars)`, `wrote apps/worker/.env (16 vars)` (more with Assistant lines you added) and `wrote apps/web/.env.local (6 vars)`.

   | File                  | Read by                                   | What is in it                                                                               |
   | --------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   | `.env.local`          | The tests, the seed and the browser tests | Everything, including the local Supabase secret key                                         |
   | `apps/api/.env`       | The API                                   | API settings. Never a secret key: the API refuses to start with one.                        |
   | `apps/worker/.env`    | The worker, and the browser tests' worker | Worker settings, the local secret key, the stand-ins, and the worker's local encryption key |
   | `apps/web/.env.local` | The web app                               | Publishable values only                                                                     |

   Each file starts with a comment saying it was generated and must not be committed, and Git ignores all four. Their values only work against the local stack.

   `pnpm env:local` rewrites all four files from scratch every time you run it. In `apps/worker/.env` it keeps `WORKER_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, which the worker seals carrier and mailbox credentials with and needs to open them later, and the Assistant's `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ASSISTANT_MODEL` and `ASSISTANT_DAILY_TOKENS` lines. Any other line you added to these files by hand is gone after the next run, so add it back afterwards. It also writes Cloudflare's always-pass Turnstile test keys (`TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY` for the worker, `NEXT_PUBLIC_TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY` for the web app), so bookings and website chats run the human check the way production does. The check goes through Cloudflare, so it needs the internet.

4. Fill the database with demo data.

   ```bash
   pnpm db:seed
   ```

   The seed reads the worker's local encryption key from `apps/worker/.env` (that one line only), so Lone Star's stand-in carrier credentials and booking links open under `pnpm dev`. Never `export` `WORKER_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in your shell: the API refuses to start while it is set.

   The seed creates the accounts through Supabase Auth and makes every change through the same command pipeline the app uses. Invitation emails go through Mailpit, and the seed accepts them from the emailed links, so the stack from step 2 must be running.

   You should see `Seeded in <n>s. Sign in at http://localhost:3000/sign-in with password HandsFree-Demo-2026:` followed by the list of accounts and the Mailpit address.

   Running the seed a second time changes nothing. It prints ``Seed data is already present (chris@gobizhelp.test exists). Run `pnpm db:reset` to start from scratch.``

Never run `pnpm db:seed`, `pnpm db:reset`, `pnpm env:local` or `pnpm test:e2e` against the hosted project. They expect Mailpit, the local Supabase stack and the stand-ins.

### Running everything

1. If your Mac restarted since last time, start Docker. (With Docker Desktop, open it instead.)

   ```bash
   colima start
   ```

2. Check whether the Supabase stack is running.

   ```bash
   pnpm supabase:status
   ```

   If it lists the local addresses, the stack is running. If it prints an error instead, start it:

   ```bash
   pnpm supabase:start
   ```

3. Start the web app, the API and the worker together.

   ```bash
   pnpm dev
   ```

   Each one reloads when its code changes. Leave this window open: it shows the logs of all three.

   You should see `OpenAPI at http://127.0.0.1:4000/docs` from the API, and a `worker started` line from the worker followed by `telephony: "fake"`, `email: "smtp"` and `mailboxes: "fake"`. That line always tells you which providers the worker is using. Check it after every change to `apps/worker/.env`.

4. Open `http://localhost:3000/sign-in` in your browser. Use `localhost`, not `127.0.0.1`: locally, passkeys only work on `localhost`.

   You should see the HandsFreeOS sign-in page.

5. Optional: check the API from Terminal.

   ```bash
   curl http://127.0.0.1:4000/healthz
   ```

   You should see a line that starts with `{"ok":true,"service":"api"` and ends with the current time.

6. Optional: check the worker the same way.

   ```bash
   curl http://127.0.0.1:4100/healthz
   ```

   You should see `{"ok":true}`.

Local addresses:

| What                  | Address                  | Notes                                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Web app               | `http://localhost:3000`  | Sign in at `/sign-in`                                                                 |
| API                   | `http://127.0.0.1:4000`  | API docs at `/docs`, health check at `/healthz`                                       |
| Worker                | `http://127.0.0.1:4100`  | Webhooks, voice tokens, number search and mailbox sign-in. Health check at `/healthz` |
| Supabase API and Auth | `http://127.0.0.1:54421` |                                                                                       |
| Supabase Studio       | `http://127.0.0.1:54423` | Browse tables, users and stored files                                                 |
| Mailpit               | `http://127.0.0.1:54424` | Every email the local stack sends                                                     |
| Postgres              | `127.0.0.1:54422`        | The apps connect as `hfos_api` and `hfos_worker`, never as `postgres`                 |
| Mailpit SMTP          | `127.0.0.1:54425`        | The worker's `SMTP_URL`                                                               |

Studio and Mailpit also answer on `localhost`. The local stack uses ports 54420 to 54429, so it does not collide with other Supabase projects on the default 543xx ports.

Local sign-in follows the same rules as the hosted project: passwords need at least 12 characters, new accounts confirm their email first, and passkeys are on. Confirmation emails (`Confirm your HandsFreeOS email`), password resets (`Reset your HandsFreeOS password`) and email changes (`Confirm your new HandsFreeOS email`) all land in Mailpit.

### What the stand-ins do

The `worker started` line names the stand-ins: `telephony: "fake"` (the fake carrier), `email: "smtp"` (Mailpit), `mailboxes: "fake"` (the mailbox stand-in), `calendars: "fake"`, `payments: "fake"` (the payment stand-in) and `push: "fake"` (the push stand-in). Production refuses every one of them.

#### The fake carrier (texts and calls)

The worker uses the fake carrier whenever `TELEPHONY_PROVIDER` is `fake` or not set, and `pnpm env:local` writes `fake`. Buying a number, carrier approval, sending, delivery receipts and call setup all happen in memory inside the worker, so nothing costs money and no phone is needed.

- **Finding a number.** In **Settings** → **Texting & calls**, **Show numbers** lists up to six made-up numbers shaped like `+1<area code>555<four digits>`: toll-free area codes 833, 844, 855 and 877, or Houston (713) for local numbers unless you type another area code.
- **Buying.** The fake carrier turns down any number that ends in `0000` with "That number is no longer available." **Show numbers** never lists one, so only the automated tests show this error.
- **Carrier approval** arrives 3 seconds after you click **Submit for approval** on the business details step (`FAKE_APPROVAL_MS=3000`). A **Legal business name** that contains `reject` is turned down with "The website does not show how customers agree to receive texts."
- **Sending.** A text shows as sent after about a quarter of a second and as delivered after about 0.7 seconds. A text whose body contains `[fail]` fails instead, with carrier error 30006.
- **RCS.** Connect `hfos_demo_agent` in the **RCS messaging** card on **Settings** → **Texting & calls** and texts go as RCS, then show as read. Texts to a customer number ending in `7` fall back to SMS or MMS. See "RCS: branded texts with buttons" in "The phone carrier: Twilio".
- **Calls from the browser** use a stand-in for Twilio's calling library. It is ready at once, and a call you place "picks up" after a moment. No sound leaves the browser.
- **Voicemail recordings** are all the same three-second, two-note chime.
- **Confirming a cell** presses 1 by itself about 2 seconds after the call is placed, so the cell is confirmed. A cell number ending in `0404` doesn't answer, and one ending in `0405` answers and presses nothing.
- **Calls through a cell** play out by themselves: the fake carrier answers the call to your cell, presses 1, rings the customer, talks for 3 seconds, hangs up and leaves a recording. Its words arrive about 15 seconds later, the same three sentences every time. A cell ending in `0404` doesn't answer, one ending in `0405` presses nothing (like a voicemail), and a customer number ending in `0486` is busy.
- **Incoming texts and calls** cannot be made by hand; only the browser tests fake them, by posting signed requests to the worker. To see what they look like, open Lone Star's seeded conversations in the inbox. They include texts, email, an unknown number, a STOP, and a voicemail with its transcript.
- **Memory resets** whenever the worker restarts, including each time `pnpm dev` reloads it after a code change. Registrations it no longer remembers then count as approved.
- **Reply reminders.** The email about an unanswered customer waits for the workspace's setting (10 minutes). To see it sooner, add `UNANSWERED_ALERT_MS=8000` to `apps/worker/.env` and restart `pnpm dev`. The next `pnpm env:local` removes that line again.

#### Mailpit (email)

- **Every email** the local stack sends lands in Mailpit at `http://127.0.0.1:54424`: sign-in emails from Supabase Auth, invitations and reminder alerts from the worker, and email a business sends to its customers. Nothing reaches a real inbox.
- **Delivery reports.** About 0.6 seconds after a business emails a customer, the worker reports the email as delivered to itself, the way Postmark would. If the first recipient's address ends in `@bounce.example.com`, it reports a hard bounce (`smtp;550 5.1.1 user unknown`) instead.
- **A business's own domain.** In **Settings** → **Email**, type the domain and click **Add domain**, then click **Check now**. It verifies at once. The DNS records it shows are placeholders (the DKIM value reads `LOCAL-DEVELOPMENT-KEY-NOT-REAL`). After a worker restart, domains it no longer remembers count as verified. A domain whose name starts with `lapsed-` (for example `lapsed-test.com`) verifies once, then stops verifying at the next check, so you can see how a lapsed domain looks. The daily check runs an hour after the worker first starts, then once a day, and its emails land in Mailpit.
- **A customer writing in** has no button either. Post a message to the worker the way Postmark's inbound webhook would. The example writes as Mike Johnson (`mike.johnson@example.com`), one of Lone Star's seeded customers. Replace `<Lone Star address>` in both places with Lone Star's address on `mail.handsfreeos.com`, shown in Lone Star's **Settings** → **Email**. The first line sets the local webhook password, a fixed value that is not a secret. If you set your own `POSTMARK_WEBHOOK_PASSWORD` in `apps/worker/.env`, use that instead.

  ```bash
  P=local-postmark-webhook-password
  curl -u "postmark:$P" \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"MessageID":"local-test-1","From":"mike.johnson@example.com","FromFull":{"Email":"mike.johnson@example.com","Name":"Mike Johnson"},"ToFull":[{"Email":"<Lone Star address>","Name":"","MailboxHash":""}],"OriginalRecipient":"<Lone Star address>","Subject":"Question about my quote","TextBody":"Can you come out on Tuesday?"}' \
    http://127.0.0.1:4100/webhooks/postmark/inbound
  ```

  You should see `{"ok":true}` and, a moment later, the email in Lone Star's inbox. Give each message a new `MessageID`: the worker keeps only the first message with a given id. A wrong login gets `403`, and mail for an address no business owns is accepted and dropped. Mail from someone who is not in **Customers** does not reach the inbox. It waits in **Settings** → **Email** under **Mail from people not in Customers**.

#### The mailbox stand-in (Outlook and Gmail)

While neither `MICROSOFT_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` nor `GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` is set in `apps/worker/.env`, nothing reaches Microsoft or Google.

1. In a workspace, open **Settings** → **Email** and click **Connect Outlook**.

   You should see a page on the worker titled "Sign in to Outlook" that reads "A stand-in for Outlook’s sign-in on this development server. No real mailbox is touched."

2. Leave **Email address** as `owner@outlook.fake` or type another address, then click **Allow**. (**Cancel** shows what happens when someone backs out.)

   You should land back on **Settings** → **Email** with the mailbox connected.

How the stand-in behaves:

- Each stand-in mailbox lives in the worker's memory and is checked every 3 seconds. Email HandsFreeOS sends through it lands in that mailbox's Sent folder. A worker restart empties it.
- To drop an email into a connected stand-in mailbox, post it to the worker. Set `account` to the address you used on the stand-in page. Send it from the address of someone in **Customers**: connected mailboxes only bring in email with people in Customers.

  ```bash
  curl -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"account":"owner@outlook.fake","from":{"address":"<customer email>","name":"<customer name>"},"subject":"Hello","text":"Is Tuesday still good?"}' \
    http://127.0.0.1:4100/test/mailboxes/deliver
  ```

  You should see a reply with a `providerMessageId`, and the email in the inbox within a few seconds. This address needs no login and only exists while the stand-in is active.

- **Connect Gmail** stays disabled with the badge "Waiting on Google’s review", even locally. To try the Gmail stand-in, add `NEXT_PUBLIC_GMAIL_ENABLED=true` to `apps/web/.env.local` and restart `pnpm dev`. Its stand-in page fills in `owner@gmail.fake`.

#### The push stand-in (phone notifications)

While `PUSH_PROVIDER` is `fake` or not set, which `pnpm env:local` leaves it, no push leaves the worker. The stand-in keeps every push it was handed in the worker's memory until the worker restarts.

- **A phone** is a row in `app.push_devices`, made when the app signs in (`push_device.register`). The pushes a moment sends it go to the stand-in instead of Expo.
- **See what it was handed** for a business. Replace `<workspace id>` with the id in the business's web address (`/app/w/<workspace id>`):

  ```bash
  curl 'http://127.0.0.1:4100/test/push/sent?workspaceId=<workspace id>'
  ```

  You should see a `sent` list: each push's phone token, whether it went as an iPhone or an Android push, its words, its category and the `data` the app reads.

- **Receipt checks** wait 15 minutes. To run them, and any push still waiting to go, now:

  ```bash
  curl -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"workspaceId":"<workspace id>"}' \
    http://127.0.0.1:4100/test/push/run-due
  ```

- **A token with `Gone` in it** (like `ExponentPushToken[Gone-1]`) is a phone the app was removed from: its receipt turns the phone off. A token with `Dead` in it is refused on the spot.
- **The phone app's test builds** register a stand-in token (`ExponentPushToken[e2e-…]`), so a moment's push for the person signed in on the simulator or emulator lands in this list. **Settings** → **Test tools** → **Test notifications** reads it back and shows it as a real push is shown (see "The phone app" under "Running the tests").
- **Real pushes to a real phone** from your laptop need `PUSH_PROVIDER=expo` and `EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN` in `apps/worker/.env`, under "Rules for real keys on a laptop".

### Trying the Assistant

Locally the worker has no Anthropic key, so its `worker started` line shows `assistant: "none"` and the Assistant panel says "The Assistant isn’t set up here yet". To try the real Assistant, give the local worker a key of its own. Its questions cost money from the same Anthropic credits, at the prices in "What it costs" in "The Assistant: Anthropic".

1. In the Claude Console, go to **Settings** → **Workspaces**, click **Create workspace**, name it `HandsFreeOS local`, and click **Create**. On its **Spend limits** tab, set a small monthly cap, for example $20.

   You should see `HandsFreeOS local` in the list of workspaces.

2. Go to **Settings** → **API keys** and click **Create key**. Name it `handsfreeos-local <your name>`, set **Linked account** to yourself, pick `HandsFreeOS local` as its only workspace, and pick an expiration of 30 days. Never use the production key on a laptop.
3. Create the key, copy it, and save it in your password manager as a new entry named "Anthropic local key".

   You should see the new key in the list on **API keys**.

4. Open `apps/worker/.env` in a plain-text editor.

   ```bash
   nano apps/worker/.env
   ```

5. Add this line at the end, with your local key in place of the placeholder and no quotes, then save with Control-O, Return and Control-X.

   ```text
   ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<Anthropic local key>
   ```

   Git ignores `apps/worker/.env`. Never commit it, and never put the key in any other file in the repository.

6. Stop `pnpm dev` with Control-C and start it again.

   You should see `assistant: "anthropic"` in the `worker started` line.

7. Sign in, open a workspace, click **Ask HandsFreeOS** in the sidebar (or press Command-J), and ask `What can you help me with here?` The first time, give your OK to use Claude ("Each person's OK" in "The Assistant: Anthropic").

   You should see the answer appear as Claude writes it.

Good to know:

- `pnpm env:local` keeps the key, and any `ASSISTANT_MODEL` or `ASSISTANT_DAILY_TOKENS` line, when it rewrites `apps/worker/.env`.
- Never `export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in your shell. The API refuses to start while it can see any name that starts with `ANTHROPIC_`, and the worker would use the shell's key instead of the one in `apps/worker/.env`.
- The daily limit of 2,000,000 tokens per workspace applies here too. To try another model or limit, add an `ASSISTANT_MODEL=` or `ASSISTANT_DAILY_TOKENS=` line the same way and restart `pnpm dev`.
- The browser tests never call Anthropic. Their worker uses a scripted stand-in and an empty key, and the empty key wins over the one in `apps/worker/.env`.
- After 30 days the key expires. Questions then end with "Something went wrong", and the `pnpm dev` window shows `assistant run failed` with `authentication_error`. Make a new local key and replace the line.

### Trying the calendar locally

While neither `MICROSOFT_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` nor `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` is set in `apps/worker/.env`, calendars use a stand-in and nothing reaches Google or Microsoft. The `worker started` line then shows `calendars: "fake"`.

1. Sign in with a seeded account, open a workspace, and open **Settings** → **My calendar**.
2. Click **Google** (or **Outlook**).

   You should see a page on the worker titled "Sign in to Google Calendar" that reads "A stand-in for Google’s sign-in on this development server. No real calendar is touched." No Google account is needed.

3. Leave **Email address** as `owner@gmail.fake` or type another address, then click **Allow**. (**Cancel** shows what happens when someone backs out.)

   You should land back on **Settings** → **My calendar** with the badge **Connected**.

How the stand-in behaves:

- Each stand-in calendar's busy times and events live in the worker's memory, and a worker restart empties them. Busy times are read every 10 minutes (`CALENDAR_REFRESH_MS`), or at once with **Sync now**.
- The worker has two test-only addresses for the stand-in. They need no login, and they exist only while the stand-in is on. To add a busy time, post it. Set `account` to the address you used on the stand-in page, and change the two times to a day in the next 60 days (they are in UTC, which is what the `Z` means).

  ```bash
  curl -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"account":"owner@gmail.fake","start":"2026-10-06T15:00:00Z","end":"2026-10-06T16:00:00Z"}' \
    http://127.0.0.1:4100/test/calendars/busy
  ```

  You should see `{"ok":true}`. Click **Sync now**, and the time shows as **Busy** in the **Calendar**.

- To see what HandsFreeOS wrote into a stand-in calendar:

  ```bash
  curl 'http://127.0.0.1:4100/test/calendars/events?account=owner@gmail.fake'
  ```

  You should see `{"events":[...]}`, one entry for each appointment that person is on, each with `"attendees":[]`.

- The booking page works locally too. Owners and admins set up the booking site in **Settings** → **Calendars** → **Booking site**, and turn on **Customers can book it online** for a calendar. Then open `http://localhost:3000/book/<site>/<calendar>`, where `<site>` is the booking site's **Link name** and `<calendar>` is the calendar's link name. The seed sets up Lone Star's site with four calendars at `http://localhost:3000/book/lone-star-hvac` ("Try booking locally" in "The calendar: Google, Outlook and online booking" walks through it). Locally each address may book ten times as often as in production, because every test comes from one address.
- The Turnstile check runs locally with Cloudflare's always-pass test keys, which `pnpm env:local` writes: the booking page shows Cloudflare's check above the **Book** button, and it passes by itself. It goes through Cloudflare, so it needs the internet. To book without it, delete the `TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY` line from `apps/worker/.env` and restart `pnpm dev`; the next `pnpm env:local` puts it back.
- Setting `MICROSOFT_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` (as in "Outlook" under "Trying a real provider from your laptop") switches calendars to the real providers too. The **Google** button then opens "Google Calendar isn’t set up yet" unless the Google Calendar values are set as well. To keep the calendar stand-in while you try real Outlook mail, also add `CALENDAR_PROVIDER=fake` to `apps/worker/.env`. `pnpm env:local` removes that line when it rewrites the file.
- A running tunnel exposes the two test addresses above, like `/test/mailboxes/deliver`.

### Trying money locally

Money runs against a payment stand-in (`apps/worker/src/payments/fake.ts`) unless you configure a real Stripe or Square application, so **no Stripe or Square account is needed** and nothing costs money. `pnpm db:reset` leaves Lone Star with two connected accounts already, a catalogue, invoices paid and overdue, estimates out, a deposit paid at booking and two plans.

- **Connecting an account.** In **Settings** → **Payments**, **Connect Stripe** and **Connect Square** open the stand-in's own sign-in page on the worker instead of the provider's, then come back the same way a real sign-in does. You can connect several, including two of the same kind, and mark one **Default**.
- **Paying.** A customer's invoice page and the deposit step open the stand-in's own payment page, where Stripe's Payment Element or Square's card field would be. Type one of these numbers:

  | Number                | What happens                                                                            |
  | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `4242 4242 4242 4242` | Goes through.                                                                           |
  | `4000 0000 0000 0002` | Refused by the card, there and then.                                                    |
  | `4000 0000 0000 0341` | Saves fine, then fails the next time something bills it without the customer there.     |
  | `4000 0000 0000 0259` | Goes through, and can then be disputed.                                                 |
  | `000123456789`        | A bank transfer. It answers "on its way" and settles when you ask (see the test route). |
  | `000111111116`        | A bank transfer the bank sends back days later.                                         |

- **Skipping time.** Three worker routes stand in for waiting, and only exist with the stand-in provider:

  ```bash
  curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4100/test/money/run-due \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"workspaceId":"<workspace id>"}'
  ```

  runs the money jobs that are waiting: reminders, overdue marks, estimates expiring, plan cycles, refunds and the token refresh. It answers `{"moved":n,"ran":{...}}`.

  ```bash
  curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4100/test/money/provider-event \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"workspaceId":"<workspace id>","paymentId":"<the provider’s payment id>","event":"settle"}'
  ```

  makes the stand-in do the thing and post its **properly signed** webhook at our own endpoint, exactly as Stripe or Square would. `event` is `settle` (a bank transfer lands), `fail_transfer` (the bank sends it back), `dispute`, `cycle` (a plan bills its next month — name `subscriptionId` instead) or `revoke` (the seller ends our access — name `accountId`).

  ```bash
  curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4100/test/money/link \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"workspaceId":"<workspace id>","invoiceId":"<invoice id>"}'
  ```

  hands back the customer's own link for a document or a plan (`estimateId`, `invoiceId` or `subscriptionId`). Those links are signed with the worker's own key, so the API can't make one: in the app, an owner or admin presses **Copy link** on the estimate, invoice or plan page, which asks the worker's signed-in `POST /v1/money/link` for the very link the customer was sent. This route is the same thing without signing in. Every email the stack sends is in Mailpit at http://localhost:54424, and the links in those work too.

- **What is real even here.** Every webhook the stand-in posts is signed with the real algorithms and goes through the real verifier; every payment's answer is read back from the provider rather than trusted from the page; card details never reach HandsFreeOS, because the stand-in's page mints a token exactly as Stripe's and Square's do. So the paths this exercises are the ones production uses.
- **Watching a hold expire.** A time held while a customer pays goes back on the calendar fifteen minutes after its deposit invoice is raised. The seed leaves one held for Gerald Tran, so open the calendar within fifteen minutes of `pnpm db:reset` to see "Not booked yet · waiting on a deposit", or run `run-due` to let it go at once.

### Running the tests

Both kinds of tests need the local stack running and `pnpm env:local` done.

**Stop the watch-mode worker first.** A `pnpm dev` (or `pnpm --filter @hfos/worker dev`) left running is the
largest single source of failures that look like bugs and are not. It claims jobs from the same database the
tests use, so a test that creates a call and then looks for it as `initiated` finds nothing, a test that counts
today's runs counts somebody else's, and an Assistant answer sits at `live` forever because the worker answering
it has no scripted stand-in configured. It restarts itself whenever a file changes, so it comes back after a
commit without anyone noticing. Check before a suite:

```bash
lsof -ti :4000,:4100,:4110,:4120
```

Nothing should answer except what you started deliberately. This matters most when more than one person, or more
than one session, is working on the same machine. The browser tests do not fail when something is already there:
they reuse it silently, whichever checkout started it. See "A git worktree is not an isolated copy" under
"Stopping and resetting".

**Kill the watcher, not just the worker, and do it before you pull.** `pnpm dev` runs the worker under
`tsx watch`, so stopping the worker leaves the watcher, which makes a new one the moment a tracked file changes —
a `git pull`, a rebase, a commit of your own. Killing the watcher leaves its child orphaned but alive, still
holding its database connection, which is what makes a later `db:reset` half-build instead of failing honestly.
So: stop the watchers first, then the workers they left behind, then check the ports are free, and only then
pull or reset. A reader who kills the children, kills the parents and then pulls ends up exactly where they
started, with three workers they think they stopped.

```bash
pkill -f 'tsx.*watch src/main.ts'; pkill -f 'pnpm --filter @hfos/worker dev'
lsof -ti :4100,:4110,:4120 | xargs -r kill -9
```

**A worker on any port but 4100 needs `WORKER_PUBLIC_URL` as well as `WORKER_HTTP_PORT`.** `pnpm env:local` writes
both `WORKER_HTTP_PORT=4100` and `WORKER_PUBLIC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4100` into `apps/worker/.env`, and a shell
variable only overrides the one you set. So `WORKER_HTTP_PORT=4120 … tsx src/main.ts` moves the listener to 4120
while the worker goes on checking Twilio's signature against `http://127.0.0.1:4100` + the path, and every webhook
the fake carrier signs for 4120 is refused with a 403 — correctly, which is what makes it read like a bug in the
app. Start it with both:

```bash
WORKER_HTTP_PORT=4120 WORKER_PUBLIC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4120 pnpm --filter @hfos/worker exec tsx src/main.ts
```

The log line at startup says which it is (`publicUrl: "http://127.0.0.1:4120"`); check it before blaming a flow.

#### Unit, database, API and worker tests

1. To be safe, stop `pnpm dev` with Control-C, so its worker does not pick up jobs the tests create.
2. Run all four suites.

   ```bash
   pnpm test
   ```
